label: def:ds
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ds}
Let $d\ge1$ and $B\subseteq Y^d$.
Two words $b,b'\in B$ are \emph{$i$-neighbors} if $b'_j=b_j$ exactly for the indices $j\neq i$.
The \emph{$i$-panel} of $b\in B$ is $\{b'\in B : b'_j=b_j\text{ for all }j\neq i\}$.
For $k\ge1$, $B$ is a \emph{$k$-pseudo-cube} of dimension $d$ if $B$ is finite and nonempty and every $i$-panel of every $b\in B$ has at least $k+1$ elements.
A $1$-pseudo-cube is a \emph{pseudo-cube}: every $b\in B$ has an $i$-neighbor in $B$ for every $i\in[d]$.
A sequence $\mathbf{x}\in X^d$ is \emph{DS-shattered} (\emph{$k$-DS-shattered}) by $\mathcal{H}$ if $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{x}}$ contains a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube ($k$-pseudo-cube).
The DS dimension $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})$ and the $k$-DS dimension $\operatorname{DS}_k(\mathcal{H})$ are the suprema of the lengths of DS-shattered and $k$-DS-shattered sequences, respectively (the supremum of the empty set is $0$).

label: def:ldim
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ldim}
A \emph{mistake tree} of depth $d$ is a complete binary tree of depth $d$ in which every internal node $v$ carries a point $x_v\in X$ and the two edges from $v$ to its children carry two distinct labels.
The tree is shattered by $\mathcal{H}$ if for every root-to-leaf path, with nodes $v_1,\dots,v_d$ and edge labels $y_1,\dots,y_d$, some $h\in\mathcal{H}$ satisfies $h(x_{v_i})=y_i$ for all $i$.
$\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})$ is the supremum of the depths of shattered mistake trees.

label: def:invariants
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:invariants}
Let $X\subseteq\Omega$ be nonempty.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item A set $A\subseteq X$ is \emph{independent} if $a\notin\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a\})$ for every $a\in A$; equivalently, $G_{(A\setminus\{a\})}$ moves $a$ for every $a\in A$.
  The \emph{height} is $\mathsf{H}_X(G)=\sup\{|A| : A\subseteq X\text{ finite and independent}\}$.
\item For $k\ge1$, the \emph{$k$-height} is $\mathsf{H}^k_X(G)=\sup\{|A| : A\subseteq X\text{ finite},\ |G_{(A\setminus\{a\})}\,a|\ge k+1\text{ for all }a\in A\}$.
  Since $a$ is moved by $G_{(A\setminus\{a\})}$ exactly when its orbit under this group has at least two points, $\mathsf{H}^1_X(G)=\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
\item A sequence $(a_1,\dots,a_k)$ in $X$ is \emph{irredundant} if $a_i\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})$ for every $i\le k$.
  $\mathsf{I}_X(G)$ is the supremum of the lengths of irredundant sequences.
\item A finite set $A\subseteq X$ is a \emph{relative base} if $X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A)$, equivalently $G_{(A)}\leG_{(X)}$.
  $\mathsf{b}_X(G)$ is the least size of a relative base ($\infty$ if there is none), and $\mathsf{B}_X(G)$ is the supremum of the sizes of the inclusion-minimal relative bases.
\end{enumerate}

label: rem:chain
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:chain}
(a) A finite independent set, listed in any order, is an irredundant sequence, because $\operatorname{cl}(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a_i\})$ by \cref{lem:closure}(b).
Hence $\mathsf{H}_X(G)\le\mathsf{I}_X(G)$.
(b) An inclusion-minimal relative base $A$ is independent.
Indeed, if $a\in\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a\})$ for some $a\in A$, then $A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a\})$ and, by \cref{lem:closure}(b,c), $X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a\})$, so $A\setminus\{a\}$ is a smaller relative base.
Hence $\mathsf{B}_X(G)\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
(c) Suppose $\mathsf{I}_X(G)<\infty$.
An irredundant sequence of maximal length cannot be extended, so every $x\in X$ lies in the closure of its points; that is, it is a relative base.
Conversely, an irredundant sequence whose points form a relative base cannot be extended.
So $\mathsf{I}_X(G)$ is the maximal length of an \emph{irredundant relative base}; for $X=\Omega$ this is the classical maximal irredundant base length.
Relative bases then exist, and a relative base of minimum size is inclusion-minimal, so $\mathsf{b}_X(G)\le\mathsf{B}_X(G)$.
In total, $\mathsf{b}_X(G)\le\mathsf{B}_X(G)\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)\le\mathsf{I}_X(G)$ whenever $\mathsf{I}_X(G)<\infty$.

label: rem:F-necessary
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:F-necessary}
Let $G=\{x\mapsto\pm x+c : c\in\mathbb{Z}\}$, the infinite dihedral group, act on $\Omega=X=\mathbb{Z}$.
Its orbits are infinite.
The pair $\{0,1\}$ is independent: $x\mapsto-x$ fixes $0$ and moves $1$, and $x\mapsto2-x$ fixes $1$ and moves $0$.
The pointwise stabilizer of two distinct points is trivial, so no $3$-set is independent and $\mathsf{H}_X(G)=2$.
For $a\neq b$ and $\delta=b-a$, the restriction of the group class to $(a,b)$ is $\mathcal{H}_{G,X}|_{(a,b)}=\{(c,c+\delta),(c,c-\delta) : c\in\mathbb{Z}\}$.
In this set the word $(c,c+\delta)$ has exactly one $1$-neighbor, $(c+2\delta,c+\delta)$, and exactly one $2$-neighbor, $(c,c-\delta)$, and the same holds for $(c,c-\delta)$ by symmetry.
So the neighbor graph is a union of bi-infinite paths, along which the first coordinate is unbounded, and no finite nonempty subset is a pseudo-cube.
Hence $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H}_{G,X})=1<2=\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.

label: lem:coset
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coset}
Let $g\in G$, let $A\subseteq X$ be finite, and let $S=S_g(A)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $V(S)=\{g'|_X : g'\in g\,G_{(A)}\}$.
\item For every $x\in X$, the set of labels $\{h(x) : h\inV(S)\}$ equals $g\big(G_{(A)}\,x\big)$.
\item All $h\inV(S)$ agree at $x\in X$ if and only if $x\in\operatorname{cl}(A)$; in that case $h(x)=gx$ for every $h\inV(S)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Version spaces are cosets

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) For $g'\in G$, the restriction $g'|_X$ is consistent with $S$ if and only if $g'a=ga$ for all $a\in A$, that is, $g^{-1}g'\inG_{(A)}$, that is, $g'\in g\,G_{(A)}$.
Every element of $V(S)\subseteq\mathcal{H}$ has the form $g'|_X$ with $g'\in G$.
(ii) By (i), the set of labels is $\{g'x : g'\in g\,G_{(A)}\}=\{gkx : k\inG_{(A)}\}=g(G_{(A)}\,x)$.
(iii) Since $g$ is a bijection, the set in (ii) is a singleton if and only if $G_{(A)}\,x=\{x\}$, that is, $x\in\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(A)})=\operatorname{cl}(A)$; the singleton is then $\{gx\}$.

label: lem:essential
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:essential}
Let $S\subseteq X$ be finite.
Then $E(S)$ is independent, so $|E(S)|\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
Moreover, every inclusion-minimal $S'\subseteq S$ with $\operatorname{cl}(S')=\operatorname{cl}(S)$ is independent; hence $\operatorname{cl}(S)=\operatorname{cl}(S')$ for an independent $S'\subseteq S$ with $|S'|\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
head: environment
name: Essential points are independent

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e\in E(S)$.
Since $E(S)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq S\setminus\{e\}$, \cref{lem:closure}(b) gives $\operatorname{cl}(E(S)\setminus\{e\})\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(S\setminus\{e\})$, and $e\notin\operatorname{cl}(S\setminus\{e\})$.
So $E(S)$ is independent.
For the second claim, let $S'\subseteq S$ be inclusion-minimal with $\operatorname{cl}(S')=\operatorname{cl}(S)$; it exists because $S$ is finite.
If $s\in\operatorname{cl}(S'\setminus\{s\})$ for some $s\in S'$, then $S'\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(S'\setminus\{s\})$, and \cref{lem:closure}(b,c) gives $\operatorname{cl}(S')\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(S'\setminus\{s\})\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(S')$.
Then $\operatorname{cl}(S'\setminus\{s\})=\operatorname{cl}(S)$, which contradicts minimality.

name: Consequences of the dictionary

label: rem:transfer
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:transfer}
Results about bases in group theory now become learning bounds.
Let $G\le S_n$ be primitive on $\Omega=[n]$ and not a primitive large-base group (a subgroup of $S_m\wr S_r$ containing $A_m^r$, in product action, with $S_m$ acting on $k$-subsets of $[m]$; see \citealp[Definition~1.2]{gill2021height}).
\citet[Theorem~1.1]{kelsey2021relational} prove that $\mathsf{I}(G)<5\log_2 n$.
By \cref{thm:dictionary}(c) and \cref{rem:chain}, the full-domain class $\mathcal{H}_{G,[n]}$ has $\operatorname{Ldim}<5\log_2 n$, and also $\operatorname{DS}<5\log_2 n$ and $\operatorname{TD}<5\log_2 n$.
By \cref{thm:erm} below, \emph{every} consistent online learner makes fewer than $5\log_2 n$ mistakes on such a class.
For the height alone, the earlier bound $\mathsf{H}(G)<9\log_2 n$ is due to \citet[Theorem~1.3]{gill2021height}.
Large-base groups are genuine exceptions: $S_n$ in its natural action has $\mathsf{I}=\mathsf{H}=n-1$ (\cref{ex:symmetric}).

name: Transfer from permutation group theory

label: ex:symmetric
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:symmetric}
Let $G=S_n$ act on $[n]$, $n\ge2$, and $X=[n]$.
For $A\subseteq[n]$, $G_{(A)}=\operatorname{Sym}([n]\setminus A)$, so $\operatorname{cl}(A)=A$ if $|A|\le n-2$ and $\operatorname{cl}(A)=[n]$ if $|A|\ge n-1$.
Hence the independent sets are the sets of size at most $n-1$, the irredundant sequences are the sequences of at most $n-1$ distinct points, and the relative bases are the sets of size at least $n-1$.
So $\mathsf{b}=\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{I}=n-1$.
For $a\in A$, the orbit $G_{(A\setminus\{a\})}\,a$ is $[n]\setminus(A\setminus\{a\})$, of size $n-|A|+1$; so $\mathsf{H}^k=n-k$ for $1\le k\le n-1$.
By \cref{thm:dictionary}, learning a permutation from a partial matching has $\operatorname{DS}=\operatorname{Ldim}=\operatorname{TD}=n-1$ and $\operatorname{DS}_k=n-k$.
Its Natarajan dimension is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ (\cref{prop:symmetric}).

name: Symmetric groups

label: ex:linear
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:linear}
Let $G=\mathrm{GL}(d,q)$ act on $\Omega=X=\mathbb{F}_q^d$, with $(d,q)\neq(1,2)$.
Then $\operatorname{cl}(A)$ is the linear span $W$ of $A$.
Indeed, a linear map that fixes $A$ fixes $W$.
Conversely, let $v\notin W$ and choose a complement $U$ of $W$ that contains $v$.
If $q\ge3$, the map that is the identity on $W$ and multiplication by some $\lambda\notin\{0,1\}$ on $U$ fixes $W$ and moves $v$.
If $q=2$ and $\dim U\ge2$, extend $v$ by some $u$ to a basis of $U$ and use the map that fixes $W$ and the other basis vectors and sends $v\mapsto v+u$.
If $q=2$ and $\dim U=1$, then $W\neq0$ because $d\ge2$; pick $w\in W\setminus\{0\}$ and use the map that fixes $W$ and sends $v\mapsto v+w$.
Hence independent sets, irredundant sequences and relative bases are linearly independent sets, linearly independent sequences and spanning sets, and $\mathsf{b}=\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{I}=d$.
Learning an invertible linear map from point correspondences therefore has $\operatorname{DS}=\operatorname{Ldim}=\operatorname{TD}=d$.
For the affine group $\mathrm{AGL}(d,q)$ acting on $\mathbb{F}_q^d$, conjugate by a translation that moves a point of a nonempty $A$ to $0$.
Affine maps that fix $0$ are linear, so the pointwise stabilizer of the translated set is its pointwise stabilizer in $\mathrm{GL}(d,q)$, whose fixed points form its linear span.
Translating back, $\operatorname{cl}(A)$ is the affine span of $A$; and $\operatorname{cl}(\emptyset)=\emptyset$ because translations fix no point.
So independent sets are affinely independent sets, relative bases are affinely spanning sets, and $\mathsf{b}=\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{I}=d+1$.

name: Linear and affine maps over a finite field

label: ex:projective
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:projective}
Let $G=\mathrm{PGL}(d+1,q)$ act on the points of the projective space $\Omega=X=\mathbb{P}^d(\mathbb{F}_q)$, with $d\ge1$ and $q\ge3$.
A frame, that is, $d+2$ points of which every $d+1$ have linearly independent representatives, is a base: in the basis given by $d+1$ of its points, an element that fixes these points is diagonal, and fixing the last point $e_0+\dots+e_d$ forces all diagonal entries to be equal.
No $d+1$ points form a base.
If their representatives are linearly independent, the diagonal map $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,1,\dots,1)$ in that basis, with $\lambda\notin\{0,1\}$, fixes them and is not scalar.
Otherwise they lie in a hyperplane $U=\ker\varphi$, and the transvection $x\mapsto x+\varphi(x)u$ with $u\in U\setminus\{0\}$ fixes them and is not scalar.
Hence $\mathsf{b}=d+2$ and, by \cref{thm:dictionary}(d), $\operatorname{TD}=d+2$: a projective transformation is taught by the images of a frame and by no set of $d+1$ points.
The same linear algebra works over every field with at least three elements; over $1.85$ and $d=2$ it is the familiar fact that four point correspondences in general position, and no three, determine a planar homography.

label: thm:erm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:erm}
Let $G\le\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$, let $X\subseteq\Omega$ be nonempty, and let $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{G,X}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{(Expected error.)}
  Let $\Omega$ be countable and $\mathsf{H}<\infty$.
  For every consistent learner $\mathcal{A}$, every distribution $D$ on $X$, every target $h^\star\in\mathcal{H}$ and every $m\ge0$,
  \[
    \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_m\sim D}\big[\operatorname{er}_D(\mathcal{A}(S_m))\big]\le\frac{\mathsf{H}}{m+1}.
  \]
\item \emph{(High probability.)}
  Let $\Omega$ be countable, $\mathsf{H}<\infty$, $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $m\ge1$.
  With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S_m\sim D^m$, \emph{every} $f\inV(S_m)$ satisfies
  \[
    \operatorname{er}_D(f)\le\frac{48}{m}\Big(\mathsf{H}\log_2880+\log_2\frac{24}{\delta}\Big).
  \]
  In particular, if $\mathsf{H}\ge1$ then $\operatorname{er}_D(f)\le c\,(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/m$ with $c=690$.
\item \emph{(Lower bound.)}
  Assume~\eqref{eq:F}.
  Call $\mathcal{H}$ \emph{nondegenerate} if there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ and $k\in G_{x_0}$ with $kx_1\neq x_1$; this holds whenever $\mathsf{H}\ge2$.
  If $\mathcal{H}$ is nondegenerate and $\mathsf{H}<\infty$, let $\varepsilon\in(0,1/16)$ and $\delta\in(0,1/8)$.
  Every learner (a deterministic map from samples to predictors, possibly improper) that uses $m$ examples and, for every distribution $D$ on $X$ and every target $h^\star\in\mathcal{H}$, outputs a predictor with $\operatorname{er}_D\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, satisfies
  \[
    m\ge\frac{(\mathsf{H}-1)\ln2+4\ln(1/\delta)}{32\,\varepsilon}.
  \]
  If $\mathsf{H}=\infty$, then $\mathcal{H}$ is not PAC learnable.
\item \emph{(Optimal rate.)}
  Consequently, if $\Omega$ is countable, \eqref{eq:F} holds, $\mathcal{H}$ is nondegenerate and $\mathsf{H}<\infty$, then for $\varepsilon\in(0,1/16)$ and $\delta\in(0,1/8)$ the least number of examples with which a deterministic learner is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-correct on all realizable pairs is $\Theta\big((\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\big)$, with absolute constants: $\lceil 690(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\rceil$ examples suffice for every consistent learner, and $(\ln 2/64)(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon$ examples are necessary.
\item \emph{(Online.)}
  Every consistent online learner makes at most $\mathsf{I}$ mistakes on every sequence that is realizable by $\mathcal{H}$.
  If $\mathsf{I}<\infty$, then every deterministic online learner errs in every round of some realizable sequence of length $\mathsf{I}$; if $\mathsf{I}=\infty$, then for every $n$ every deterministic online learner errs in every round of some realizable sequence of length $n$.
\end{enumerate}

label: rem:computation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:computation}
(a) Let $\Omega=[n]$ and let $G$ be given by a set of generating permutations.
The Schreier--Sims algorithm computes, in time polynomial in $n$ and the number of generators, a stabilizer chain $G=G^{(0)}\ge G^{(1)}\ge\dots\ge G^{(k)}$ with $G^{(i)}=G_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_i\})}$ along any prescribed sequence of points, together with transversals of each $G^{(i)}$ in $G^{(i-1)}$ \citep[Chapter~4]{seress2003permutation}.
Given a sample $S_g(A)$ with $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$, one finds a consistent hypothesis level by level.
Suppose $g'_{i-1}$ agrees with $g$ on $a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}$.
Then $g_{i-1}'^{-1}g\in G^{(i-1)}$, so the point $y=g_{i-1}'^{-1}ga_i$ lies in the orbit $G^{(i-1)}a_i$.
If $t\in G^{(i-1)}$ is the transversal element with $ta_i=y$, then $g'_i=g'_{i-1}t$ agrees with $g$ on $a_1,\dots,a_i$.
So consistent learning, and hence by \cref{thm:erm} optimal PAC and online learning, is computationally efficient for permutation groups given by generators.
(b) Agnostic ERM for $S_n$ acting on $[n]$ is a maximum-weight bipartite matching problem.
Given a sample $((x_i,y_i))_{i\le m}$, put $c(x,y)=|\{i : (x_i,y_i)=(x,y)\}|$; a permutation $\pi$ maximizes the number of correctly labeled examples if and only if it maximizes $\sum_{x\in[n]}c(x,\pi(x))$, which is the assignment problem on the complete bipartite graph with vertex classes $[n]$ and $[n]$, solvable in polynomial time.
Whether agnostic ERM is tractable for other group classes is discussed in \cref{sec:discussion}.

label: rem:profinite
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:profinite}
Let $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ be a separable closure of a countable field $K$ (so $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is countable) and let $G=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K)$ act on $\Omega=X=K^{\mathrm{sep}}$.
The orbit of $\alpha$ is its set of conjugates over $K$, which is finite, so~\eqref{eq:F} holds and \cref{thm:dictionary} applies.
For $K=\mathbb{Q}$ the class is not PAC learnable.
Indeed, let $P$ be a finite set of primes and $p\in P$.
By the classical fact quoted above, $\sqrt p\notin F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt r : r\in P\setminus\{p\})$, so $F(\sqrt p)/F$ has an automorphism that fixes $F$ and sends $\sqrt p$ to $-\sqrt p$.
This automorphism extends to an element of $G$ \citep[Chapter~V]{lang2002algebra}, which fixes every $\sqrt r$ with $r\in P\setminus\{p\}$ and moves $\sqrt p$.
So $\{\sqrt p : p\in P\}$ is independent for every finite $P$, and $\mathsf{H}_X(G)=\infty$.
By \cref{thm:dictionary}(a) and \cref{thm:erm}(c), $\operatorname{DS}=\infty$ and the class is not PAC learnable; by \cref{rem:chain}(a), also $\operatorname{Ldim}=\infty$.
Yet by \cref{lem:coset}(ii) and~\eqref{eq:F}, after every finite sample each point has only finitely many candidate labels.

label: thm:natarajan
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:natarajan}
Let $G\le\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$, let $X\subseteq\Omega$ be nonempty, and let $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{G,X}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Every N-shattered sequence in $X$ consists of distinct points that form an independent set.
  Hence $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$; under~\eqref{eq:F}, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})\le\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})=\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
\item \emph{(Commuting moves.)}
  Let $A\subseteq X$ be finite, and suppose that there are pairwise commuting elements $k_a\inG_{(A\setminus\{a\})}$ with $k_aa\neq a$, for $a\in A$.
  Then $A$, in any order, is N-shattered by $\mathcal{H}$, with $f_0(a)=a$ and $f_1(a)=k_aa$.
\item If $G$ is abelian, then $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})=\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
  For every abelian subgroup $K\le G$, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})\ge\mathsf{H}_X(K)$, the height of $K$ acting on $\Omega$, relative to $X$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Commuting moves give Natarajan shattering

label: ex:linear-natarajan
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:linear-natarajan}
Let $G=\mathrm{GL}(d,q)$ act on $\mathbb{F}_q^d$ as in \cref{ex:linear}.
If $q\ge3$, let $K$ be the group of diagonal matrices with respect to a basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$.
The elements of $K$ that fix $e_j$ for $j\neq i$ are the matrices $\mathrm{diag}(1,\dots,\lambda,\dots,1)$, which move $e_i$ when $\lambda\neq1$.
So $\{e_1,\dots,e_d\}$ is independent for the action of $K$ (each $e_i$ is moved by an element of $K$ that fixes the others), and \cref{thm:natarajan}(iii) gives $\operatorname{Nat}=d=\operatorname{DS}$.
Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the diagonal group is trivial, and the Natarajan dimension can drop: for $\mathrm{GL}(3,2)$ acting on the $7$ nonzero vectors of $\mathbb{F}_2^3$, exhaustive computation gives $\operatorname{Nat}=2<3=\mathsf{H}$.

label: rem:abelian-strict
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:abelian-strict}
Let $S_3$ act on $\{0,1,2\}$ naturally and on $\{3,4\}$ through the sign, so that odd permutations swap $3$ and $4$.
The sequence $(0,3)$ is N-shattered with $f_0=(0,3)$ and $f_1=(1,4)$: the four patterns are realized by $\mathrm{id}$, by $(1\,2)$, by $(0\,1\,2)$ and by $(0\,1)$.
So $\operatorname{Nat}=\mathsf{H}=2$.
Every abelian subgroup is cyclic of order $2$ or $3$, and the stabilizer of a moved point in such a subgroup is trivial; so every abelian subgroup has height $1$.
Similarly, $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ acting on the $8$ points of the projective line over $\mathbb{F}_7$ has $\mathsf{H}=3$ and $\operatorname{Nat}=2$, while all its abelian subgroups have height $1$ (exhaustive computation).

Let $\Omega$ be finite and $G\le\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$.
Suppose that the closure $\operatorname{cl}(S)=\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(S)})$ satisfies the exchange property: for all $S\subseteq\Omega$ and $p,q\in\Omega$, if $q\in\operatorname{cl}(S\cup\{p\})\setminus\operatorname{cl}(S)$, then $p\in\operatorname{cl}(S\cup\{q\})$.

label: def:monodromy
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:monodromy}
A $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube $B\subseteq Y^d$ is \emph{two-fibered} if every $b\in B$ has exactly one $i$-neighbor in $B$ for each $i\in[d]$; we denote it by $s_i(b)$.
The \emph{monodromy group} of $B$ is the permutation group $M=M(B)=\langle s_1,\dots,s_d\rangle\le\operatorname{Sym}(B)$.
Its \emph{parabolic subgroups} are $K_i=\langle s_j : j\neq i\rangle$, for $i\in[d]$.
We write $\pi_j\colon B\to Y$, $b\mapsto b_j$, for the coordinate maps.
head: environment
name: Two-fibered pseudo-cubes and their monodromy

label: thm:monodromy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:monodromy}
Let $B\subseteq Y^d$ be a two-fibered $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube with monodromy group $M$ and parabolic subgroups $K_1,\dots,K_d$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Each $s_i$ is a fixed-point-free involution of $B$.
  Each $\pi_j$ is constant on $K_j$-orbits, and $\pi_j(s_jb)\neq\pi_j(b)$.
  In particular $s_jb\notin K_j\cdot b$ \textup{(separation)}, and $s_j\notin K_j$.
\item \emph{(Orbit labels.)}
  The map $\iota\colon b\mapsto(K_1\cdot b,\dots,K_d\cdot b)$ is injective.
  Its image $B^\sharp$ is a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube in which $\iota(s_ib)$ is an $i$-neighbor of $\iota(b)$, and $B$ is the image of $B^\sharp$ under the coordinatewise maps $K_j\cdot b\mapsto\pi_j(b)$.
\item \emph{(Galois closure.)}
  Assume that $M$ is transitive on $B$, and fix $b_0\in B$.
  Let $C=\{(K_1m,\dots,K_dm) : m\in M\}$, with right cosets.
  Then $C$ is a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube; after the relabeling $m\mapsto m^{-1}$ it is the coset complex $\mathcal{C}_M(K_1,\dots,K_d)$.
  The coordinatewise maps $K_jm\mapsto K_j\cdot(mb_0)$ are well defined and map $C$ onto $B^\sharp$, sending the word $(K_jm)_{j}$ to $\iota(mb_0)$.
  If moreover $M$ acts regularly on $B$, these maps are bijections, and $C\cong B^\sharp$.
\item \emph{(Abelian monodromy.)}
  $M$ is abelian if and only if $B$ is a disjoint union of sets of the form $\prod_{j=1}^d\{u_j,v_j\}$ with $u_j\neq v_j$ (full Natarajan cubes).
  In that case these sets are exactly the $M$-orbits, and $M$ is an elementary abelian $2$-group.
\item \emph{(Local version.)}
  If $T\subseteq[d]$, $b\in B$, and the involutions $s_i$ $(i\in T)$ pairwise commute on the orbit $O=\langle s_i : i\in T\rangle\cdot b$, then the projection of $O$ to the coordinates in $T$ is the Natarajan cube $\prod_{j\in T}\{\pi_j(b),\pi_j(s_jb)\}$.
  Hence $\operatorname{Nat}(B)\ge|T|$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Monodromy of two-fibered pseudo-cubes

label: rem:orbits
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:orbits}
Each $M$-orbit $O\subseteq B$ is closed under every $s_i$, so every word of $O$ has its unique $i$-neighbor inside $O$.
Thus $O$ is itself a two-fibered $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube, whose monodromy group is the restriction of $M$ to $O$ and is transitive.
Since $B$ is the disjoint union of its $M$-orbits, part (c) describes every two-fibered pseudo-cube, one orbit at a time.
head: environment
name: Transitivity is no restriction

label: rem:regular
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:regular}
By (b), $\iota$ is a bijection from $B$ onto $B^\sharp$ that maps $i$-neighbors to $i$-neighbors, and $B$ is obtained from $B^\sharp$ by a coordinatewise relabeling.
So when $M$ acts regularly, (c) and (b) together show that the map $(K_jm)_j\mapsto mb_0$ is a bijection from $C$ onto $B$ that maps $i$-neighbors to $i$-neighbors for every $i$, and that is induced by coordinatewise relabelings.
In this sense $B$ is the coset complex of its monodromy group, up to coordinatewise relabeling of the labels.

label: ex:biquadratic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:biquadratic}
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and $L=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$, of degree $4$.
The group $\Gamma=\{1,\sigma,\tau,\sigma\tau\}\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ consists of the identity, $\sigma\colon\sqrt2\mapsto-\sqrt2,\ \sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3$, $\tau\colon\sqrt2\mapsto\sqrt2,\ \sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3$, and $\sigma\tau$.
Its five subgroups $1$, $\langle\sigma\rangle$, $\langle\tau\rangle$, $\langle\sigma\tau\rangle$, $\Gamma$ correspond to the five intermediate fields $L$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt6)$, $\mathbb{Q}$.
This is the field of \cref{fig:hero}(a) and of the example in \cref{sec:fields}.
More generally, for distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_r$ the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_r})$ has degree $2^r$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ \citep[Theorem~5.30 and Example~5.31(b)]{milne2022fields}, and its Galois group is $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^r$.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:finitefields}
For a prime power $q$ and $n\ge1$, the extension $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$ is Galois, and its group is cyclic of order $n$, generated by the Frobenius map $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^q$.
Its intermediate fields are the fields $\mathbb F_{q^d}$ with $d\mid n$.

label: ex:cubic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:cubic}
Let $L=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]2,\omega)$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, the splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Then $[L:\mathbb{Q}]=6$, and $\Gamma\cong S_3$ acts faithfully on the three roots $\sqrt[3]2$, $\omega\sqrt[3]2$, $\omega^2\sqrt[3]2$.
The stabilizer of the root $\sqrt[3]2$ has order $2$ and fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]2)$, of degree $3$; the subgroup $A_3$ has fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(\omega)=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$, of degree $2$.
On the three roots alone, the class is $S_3$ acting on three points, which has Natarajan dimension $1$ and DS dimension $2$ (\cref{prop:symmetric}(b), \cref{thm:dictionary}(a), and the hexagon of \cref{fig:hexagon}); on the whole field $L$, $\operatorname{Nat}=\operatorname{DS}=\mu(S_3)=2$ (\cref{thm:solvable}(a)).

label: fact:conjugates
title: Fact
head: environment
name: Conjugates

title: Proof
body_md:
Each $\sigma\in\Gamma$ maps roots of $f$ to roots of $f$, since $f$ has coefficients in $K$.
The polynomial $g=\prod_{\beta\in\Gamma\alpha}(x-\beta)$ has distinct roots, and its coefficients are fixed by every $\sigma\in\Gamma$, since $\sigma$ permutes $\Gamma\alpha$; so $g\in L^\Gamma[x]=K[x]$.
As $g(\alpha)=0$, $f$ divides $g$; so $f$ has distinct roots, and they lie in $\Gamma\alpha$.
Conversely every point of $\Gamma\alpha$ is a root of $f$.
Hence $f=g$ and $|\Gamma\alpha|=\deg f=[K(\alpha):K]$.
Finally, $\sigma$ fixes $\alpha$ if and only if it fixes $K(\alpha)$ pointwise.

label: ex:quartic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:quartic}
Let $L=\mathbb{Q}(x_1,\dots,x_4)$, $\Gamma=S_4$ and $K=L^{S_4}$.
The group $S_4$ permutes the three elements $\theta_1=x_1x_2+x_3x_4$, $\theta_2=x_1x_3+x_2x_4$ and $\theta_3=x_1x_4+x_2x_3$, which are the roots of the resolvent cubic, and the kernel of this action is $V_4=\{1,(1\,2)(3\,4),(1\,3)(2\,4),(1\,4)(2\,3)\}$.
The element $\sqrt{\mathrm{disc}}=\prod_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)$ has stabilizer $A_4$.
By the fundamental theorem, the tower
\[
K\ \subset\ K(\sqrt{\mathrm{disc}})\ \subset\ K(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)\ \subset\ L
\]
corresponds to the chief series (defined below) $S_4>A_4>V_4>1$, and its steps have degrees $2$, $3$ and $4$.
The classical solution follows this tower: a square root, then the roots of the resolvent cubic, then square roots.
The three points used in \cref{sec:solvable} and \cref{fig:quartic} are $\sqrt{\mathrm{disc}}$, $\theta_1$ and $x_4$; their stabilizers $A_4$, $D_4$ and $S_3$ are the subgroups $C$ that complement the three chief factors, whereas the tower above uses the members of the series.

\label{ext:ftgt}
Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension with group $\Gamma$.
For every intermediate field $K\subseteq F\subseteq L$, the extension $L/F$ is Galois.
The maps $F\mapsto\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)$ and $U\mapsto L^U$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections between the intermediate fields of $L/K$ and the subgroups of $\Gamma$, and $[L:L^U]=|U|$ for every subgroup $U\le\Gamma$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For a sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_d)$ in $X$ and $g\in G$, write $w(g)=(ga_1,\dots,ga_d)$, so that $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}=\{w(g) : g\in G\}$.
Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_d\}$.

\emph{(a), shattered implies distinct and independent.}
Let $B\subseteq\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ be a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube.
For $d=1$ there is nothing to prove about distinctness.
If $d\ge2$ and $a_i=a_j$ for some $i\neq j$, then every word of $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ has equal $i$-th and $j$-th coordinates; an $i$-neighbor $b'$ of $b\in B$ changes coordinate $i$ but not coordinate $j$, which is impossible.
For independence, fix $i$, pick $b=w(g)\in B$, and pick an $i$-neighbor $b'=w(g')\in B$.
Then $g'a_j=ga_j$ for $j\neq i$ and $g'a_i\neq ga_i$.
So $k\coloneqq g^{-1}g'\inG_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})}$ and $ka_i\neq a_i$, that is, $a_i\notin\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})})=\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a_i\})$.
This direction does not use~\eqref{eq:F}.

\emph{(a), distinct and independent implies that $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ is a pseudo-cube.}
$\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ is nonempty, and it is finite because it is contained in $\prod_iGa_i$, which is finite by~\eqref{eq:F}.
Let $b=w(g)$ and $i\in[d]$.
By independence there is $k\inG_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})}$ with $ka_i\neq a_i$.
The word $w(gk)$ agrees with $w(g)$ at every $j\neq i$, since $gka_j=ga_j$, and differs from it at $i$, since $g$ is injective and $ka_i\neq a_i$.
So $w(gk)$ is an $i$-neighbor of $b$ in $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$.

\emph{(a), the dimension.}
By the first step, every DS-shattered sequence of length $d$ yields an independent $d$-subset of $X$, so $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
By the second step, every finite independent subset of $X$, listed in any order, is DS-shattered, so $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})\ge\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
Both sides are suprema over the same set of lengths, so they agree, including the value $+\infty$.

\emph{(b).}
Assume the entries of $\mathbf{a}$ are distinct.
The $i$-panel of $w(g)$ in $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ is $\{w(g') : g'a_j=ga_j\text{ for all }j\neq i\}=\{w(gu) : u\inG_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})}\}$.
Its elements agree outside coordinate $i$ and are distinguished by their $i$-th coordinates $gua_i$; since $g$ is injective, the panel has exactly $|G_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})}\,a_i|$ elements.
($\Leftarrow$) If all these orbits have at least $k+1$ points, then $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$, which is finite by~\eqref{eq:F} and nonempty, is a $k$-pseudo-cube.
($\Rightarrow$) Let $B\subseteq\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$ be a $k$-pseudo-cube.
Every panel of $B$ has at least two elements, so $B$ is a pseudo-cube and the entries of $\mathbf{a}$ are distinct by part (a).
For $b=w(g)\in B$, the $i$-panel of $b$ in $B$ is contained in its $i$-panel in $\mathcal{H}|_{\mathbf{a}}$, so $|G_{(A\setminus\{a_i\})}\,a_i|\ge k+1$.
The equality $\operatorname{DS}_k(\mathcal{H})=\mathsf{H}^k_X(G)$ follows as in (a).

\emph{(c), $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\ge\mathsf{I}_X(G)$.}
Let $(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be irredundant.
Consider the complete binary tree of depth $r$ in which every node at depth $i-1$ carries the point $a_i$.
We label its edges so that every node at depth $i-1$ is reached by a path with labels $(y_1,\dots,y_{i-1})$ that is realized by some $g\in G$, that is, $y_j=ga_j$ for $j<i$.
At the root the path is empty, and every $g\in G$ realizes it.
At a node reached by a path realized by $g$, the labels of $a_i$ that are consistent with the path form the set $g(G_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})}\,a_i)$, by \cref{lem:coset}(ii).
This set has at least two elements because $a_i\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})$.
Choose two distinct elements $gka_i$ and $gk'a_i$, with $k,k'\inG_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})}$, as the labels of the two edges leaving the node.
The two children are then reached by paths realized by $gk$ and by $gk'$, because $k$ and $k'$ fix $a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}$.
By induction every root-to-leaf path is realized, so the tree is shattered and $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\ge r$.

\emph{(c), $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le\mathsf{I}_X(G)$.}
Let a shattered mistake tree of depth $r$ be given, and fix a root-to-leaf path with points $z_1,\dots,z_r$, whose edge labels are realized by some $g\in G$, that is, they are $gz_1,\dots,gz_r$.
At the $i$-th node, each of the two out-edge labels, together with the labels of the path prefix, is realized by some hypothesis (take any leaf below that edge).
The prefix labels are those of $g$, so by \cref{lem:coset}(ii) the labels of $z_i$ that are consistent with the prefix form the set $g(G_{(\{z_1,\dots,z_{i-1}\})}\,z_i)$.
This set contains the two distinct out-edge labels, so it has at least two elements, and $z_i\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{z_1,\dots,z_{i-1}\})$.
Hence $(z_1,\dots,z_r)$ is irredundant and $r\le\mathsf{I}_X(G)$.

\emph{(d).}
Let $h=g|_X$.
By \cref{lem:coset}(i), $V(S_g(A))=\{g'|_X : g'\in g\,G_{(A)}\}$.
This set equals $\{h\}$ if and only if $(gk)|_X=g|_X$ for every $k\inG_{(A)}$.
Since $g$ is injective, this holds if and only if every $k\inG_{(A)}$ fixes every $x\in X$, that is, $X\subseteq\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(A)})=\operatorname{cl}(A)$.
The condition does not involve $g$, so all hypotheses have the same teaching sets, and $\operatorname{TD}(h)=\min\{|A| : A\text{ a relative base}\}=\mathsf{b}_X(G)$, which is $\infty$ if there is no relative base.
A teaching set is inclusion-minimal if and only if it is an inclusion-minimal relative base, so the supremum of the sizes of the inclusion-minimal teaching sets is $\mathsf{B}_X(G)$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:closed-sets}
Let $G\le\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$, let $X\subseteq\Omega$ be nonempty, and let $\mathcal{K}=\{C\subseteq X : \operatorname{cl}_X(C)=C\}$ be the family of closed subsets of $X$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $X\in\mathcal{K}$, and $\mathcal{K}$ is closed under arbitrary intersections.
\item For $B\subseteq X$, the set $\operatorname{cl}_X(B)$ is the smallest member of $\mathcal{K}$ that contains $B$.
\item A finite $T\subseteq X$ is shattered by $\mathcal{K}$ if and only if $T$ is independent.
  Hence the VC dimension of $\mathcal{K}$ is $\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.
\end{enumerate}

name: Closed sets

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) $\operatorname{cl}_X(X)=X$ because $\operatorname{cl}$ is extensive (\cref{lem:closure}(a)).
If $C_\alpha\in\mathcal{K}$ for all $\alpha$ and $C=\bigcap_\alpha C_\alpha$, then by monotonicity $\operatorname{cl}(C)\cap X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_\alpha)\cap X=C_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$, so $\operatorname{cl}(C)\cap X\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C)\cap X$.

(b) The set $\operatorname{cl}_X(B)$ contains $B$.
It is closed: by monotonicity and idempotence (\cref{lem:closure}(b,c)), $\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}(B)\cap X)\cap X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}(B))\cap X=\operatorname{cl}(B)\cap X$, and the reverse inclusion is extensivity.
If $C\in\mathcal{K}$ contains $B$, then $\operatorname{cl}(B)\cap X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C)\cap X=C$.

(c) ($\Leftarrow$) Let $T$ be independent and $U\subseteq T$.
If $t\in T\setminus U$, then $\operatorname{cl}(U)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(T\setminus\{t\})$, which does not contain $t$.
So $\operatorname{cl}_X(U)\cap T=U$, and the closed set $\operatorname{cl}_X(U)$ cuts out $U$ from $T$.
($\Rightarrow$) Let $T$ be shattered and $t\in T$.
Pick $C\in\mathcal{K}$ with $C\cap T=T\setminus\{t\}$.
By (b), $\operatorname{cl}_X(T\setminus\{t\})\subseteq C$, and $t\in X\setminus C$, so $t\notin\operatorname{cl}(T\setminus\{t\})$.
The VC dimension is the supremum of the sizes of shattered finite sets, which is $\mathsf{H}_X(G)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout, $h^\star=g|_X$ is the target.
In (a), (b) and (d), $\Omega$ is countable, so all subsets of $\Omega$ and of its finite powers are measurable, and Fubini's theorem applies to the product measure $D^{m+1}$.

\emph{(a).}
Let $x_1,\dots,x_{m+1}$ be i.i.d.\ from $D$, and write $T_j=\{x_i : i\le m+1,\ i\neq j\}$, as a set.

Step 1 (consistent implies correct on the closure).
By \cref{lem:coset}(iii), every $f\inV(S_m)$ satisfies $f(x)=h^\star(x)$ for every $x\in\operatorname{cl}(\{x_1,\dots,x_m\})\cap X$.
Hence $\mathbf{1}[\mathcal{A}(S_m)(x_{m+1})\neq h^\star(x_{m+1})]\le\mathbf{1}[x_{m+1}\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_{m+1})]$.

Step 2 (Fubini).
$\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{er}_D(\mathcal{A}(S_m))]=\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}(S_m)(x_{m+1})\neq h^\star(x_{m+1})]\le\mathbb{P}[x_{m+1}\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_{m+1})]$.

Step 3 (exchangeability).
The joint law of $(x_1,\dots,x_{m+1})$ is invariant under permutations of the indices, and the event $\{x_j\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_j)\}$ is the image of the event $\{x_{m+1}\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_{m+1})\}$ under the transposition of $j$ and $m+1$.
So $\mathbb{P}[x_{m+1}\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_{m+1})]=\frac{1}{m+1}\mathbb{E}[Z]$, where $Z=|\{j\le m+1 : x_j\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_j)\}|$.

Step 4 (counting).
Let $S=\{x_1,\dots,x_{m+1}\}$, as a set.
If $j$ is counted in $Z$, then $x_j\neq x_i$ for all $i\neq j$, since otherwise $x_j\in T_j\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(T_j)$.
So $T_j=S\setminus\{x_j\}$ and $x_j\in E(S)$, the set of essential points of $S$.
Distinct counted indices give distinct points, because each counted point occurs exactly once in the sequence.
Hence $Z\le|E(S)|\le\mathsf{H}$ by \cref{lem:essential}.
Combining the steps, $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{er}_D(\mathcal{A}(S_m))]\le\mathsf{H}/(m+1)$.

\emph{(b).}
If $\mathsf{H}=0$, no singleton $\{x\}$ with $x\in X$ is independent, that is, $X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\emptyset)=\operatorname{Fix}(G)$.
Then \cref{lem:coset}(iii) with $A=\emptyset$ forces every label, so every $f\inV(S_m)$ equals $h^\star$ and $\operatorname{er}_D(f)=0$.
Assume $\mathsf{H}\ge1$ from now on.
Consider the binary learning problem with concept class $\mathcal{K}$ of \cref{lem:closed-sets}, target concept $X\in\mathcal{K}$ and distribution $D$; every example is labeled positive.
The closure algorithm outputs the intersection of all concepts that are consistent with the sample, which by \cref{lem:closed-sets}(b) is $\operatorname{cl}_X(\{x_1,\dots,x_m\})$.
\citet{darnstadt2015optimal} analyzes this hypothesis for every concept class on a nonempty set that is closed under intersections of arbitrary subfamilies (Theorem~8 in the author's preprint, with the explicit constants of its proof): if the class has VC dimension $d$, then for every target concept, every distribution and every $m>0$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ the closure hypothesis has error at most $\frac{48}{m}(d\log880+\log(24/\delta))$.
By \cref{lem:closed-sets}, $\mathcal{K}$ satisfies the hypotheses with $d=\mathsf{H}$.
Since $\log_bx\le\log_2x$ for every $x\ge1$ and every base $b\ge2$, the same bound holds with $\log_2$, whichever base the analysis uses.
So with probability at least $1-\delta$,
\[
  D\big(X\setminus\operatorname{cl}_X(\{x_1,\dots,x_m\})\big)\le\frac{48}{m}\Big(\mathsf{H}\log_2880+\log_2\frac{24}{\delta}\Big).
\]
On this event, every $f\inV(S_m)$ agrees with $h^\star$ on $\operatorname{cl}_X(\{x_1,\dots,x_m\})$ by \cref{lem:coset}(iii), so $\operatorname{er}_D(f)$ is at most the left-hand side.
The event does not depend on $f$, so the bound holds simultaneously for all $f\inV(S_m)$.
For the second form, $\log_2(24/\delta)=\log_224+\log_2(1/\delta)$ and $\mathsf{H}\log_2880+\log_224\le\mathsf{H}(\log_2880+\log_224)\le14.37\,\mathsf{H}$ since $\mathsf{H}\ge1$; and $48\cdot14.37\le690$.

\emph{(c).}
If $\mathsf{H}\ge2$, take an independent set $\{a,b\}\subseteq X$; independence says that $G_{(\{b\})}$ moves $a$, so $x_0=b$, $x_1=a$ and a suitable $k\in G_b$ witness nondegeneracy.
Our condition is exactly the nondegeneracy condition of \citet{hanneke2024improved}: there are $h_1,h_2\in\mathcal{H}$ and $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $h_1(x_0)=h_2(x_0)$ and $h_1(x_1)\neq h_2(x_1)$.
Indeed, for $h_1=g_1|_X$ and $h_2=g_2|_X$ this says that $k\coloneqq g_1^{-1}g_2\in G_{x_0}$ and $kx_1\neq x_1$, because $g_1$ is injective; conversely, take $g_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $g_2=k$.
By \cref{thm:dictionary}(a), $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})=\mathsf{H}$.

\citet[Theorem~2.5, with $k=1$]{hanneke2024improved} use the following definitions.
Let $\mathrm{RE}(\mathcal{H})$ be the set of distributions $P$ on $X\times Y$ with $\inf_{f\in\mathcal{H}}\operatorname{er}_P(f)=0$.
For a learner $\mathcal{A}'$, let $M_{\mathcal{A}',\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$ be the least $n$ such that $\mathbb{P}_{S\sim P^{m'}}[\operatorname{er}_P(\mathcal{A}'(S))>\varepsilon]\le\delta$ for all $m'\ge n$ and all $P\in\mathrm{RE}(\mathcal{H})$, and let $M^{\mathrm{HMZ}}_{\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$ be the infimum of $M_{\mathcal{A}',\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$ over all learners.
They prove that for every nondegenerate class of DS dimension $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $\varepsilon\in(0,1/16)$, $\delta\in(0,1/8)$,
\[
  M^{\mathrm{HMZ}}_{\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\ge\frac{(d-1)\ln2+4\ln(1/\delta)}{32\,\varepsilon}.
\]

Our learners succeed at one sample size $m$ and on exactly realizable pairs, so we need a bridge.
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a learner as in (c), and fix $\eta>0$ with $\varepsilon+\eta<1/16$ and $\delta+m\eta<1/8$.
Let $P\in\mathrm{RE}(\mathcal{H})$ with marginal $P_X$ on $X$, and pick $f_\eta\in\mathcal{H}$ with $\operatorname{er}_P(f_\eta)<\eta$.
Draw $(x_i,y_i)\sim P$ i.i.d.\ for $i\le m$, and set $S=((x_i,y_i))_{i\le m}$ and $S'=((x_i,f_\eta(x_i)))_{i\le m}$.
Then $S'$ is a sample from the exactly realizable pair $(P_X,f_\eta)$, and $\mathbb{P}[S\neq S']\le\sum_{i\le m}\mathbb{P}[y_i\neq f_\eta(x_i)]\le m\eta$.
For every predictor $f$, writing $\operatorname{er}_{P_X}(f;f_\eta)$ for the error of $f$ with respect to the target $f_\eta$,
\[
  \operatorname{er}_P(f)\le\mathbb{P}[f(x)\neq f_\eta(x)]+\mathbb{P}[f_\eta(x)\neq y]<\operatorname{er}_{P_X}(f;f_\eta)+\eta .
\]
Hence
\[
  \mathbb{P}\big[\operatorname{er}_P(\mathcal{A}(S))>\varepsilon+\eta\big]\le\mathbb{P}[S\neq S']+\mathbb{P}\big[\operatorname{er}_{P_X}(\mathcal{A}(S');f_\eta)>\varepsilon\big]\le m\eta+\delta .
\]
Let $\mathcal{A}'$ be the learner that, on a sample of size $m'\ge m$, runs $\mathcal{A}$ on its first $m$ examples.
The bound holds for $\mathcal{A}'$ at every $m'\ge m$ and every $P\in\mathrm{RE}(\mathcal{H})$, so $M^{\mathrm{HMZ}}_{\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon+\eta,\delta+m\eta)\le m$.
The theorem of \citet{hanneke2024improved} at $(\varepsilon+\eta,\delta+m\eta)$, with $d=\mathsf{H}$, gives
\[
  m\ge\frac{(\mathsf{H}-1)\ln2+4\ln\big(1/(\delta+m\eta)\big)}{32(\varepsilon+\eta)} .
\]
The right-hand side is continuous in $\eta$; letting $\eta\to0$ with $m$ fixed gives the bound of (c).
If $\mathsf{H}=\infty$, then $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})=\infty$ by \cref{thm:dictionary}(a), and a class of infinite DS dimension is not PAC learnable \citep{brukhim2022characterization}.

\emph{(d).}
A nondegenerate class has $\mathsf{H}\ge1$: the point $x_1$ is moved by $k\in G$, so $x_1\notin\operatorname{Fix}(G)=\operatorname{cl}(\emptyset)$ and $\{x_1\}$ is independent.
Upper bound: by (b), every consistent learner reaches error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ from $m=\lceil c(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\rceil$ examples.
Lower bound: the bound of (c) equals $\frac{(\mathsf{H}-1)\ln2}{32\,\varepsilon}+\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{8\,\varepsilon}$, and $\ln(1/\delta)=\ln2\cdot\log_2(1/\delta)$.
If $\mathsf{H}\ge2$, then $\mathsf{H}-1\ge\mathsf{H}/2$, so $\frac{(\mathsf{H}-1)\ln2}{32}\ge\frac{\mathsf{H}\ln2}{64}$; also $\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{8}\ge\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{64}=\frac{\ln2\cdot\log_2(1/\delta)}{64}$.
Adding the two inequalities, the bound of (c) is at least $\frac{\ln2}{64}(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon$.
If $\mathsf{H}=1$, the bound of (c) is $\ln(1/\delta)/(8\varepsilon)$.
Since $\delta<1/8$, we have $\ln(1/\delta)>\ln8>\ln2$, so
\[
  \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{8}=\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{64}+\frac{7\ln(1/\delta)}{64}\ge\frac{\ln2\cdot\log_2(1/\delta)}{64}+\frac{\ln2}{64}=\frac{\ln2}{64}\big(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta)\big),
\]
and the bound of (c) is again at least $\frac{\ln2}{64}(\mathsf{H}+\log_2(1/\delta))/\varepsilon$.
Hence $M_{\mathcal{H}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\Theta((\mathsf{H}+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)$, and every consistent learner attains this rate.

\emph{(e).}
Let the realizable sequence be labeled by $h^\star=g|_X$.
If at round $t$ we have $x_t\in\operatorname{cl}(\{x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}\})$, then by \cref{lem:coset}(iii) every hypothesis consistent with the first $t-1$ examples predicts $gx_t$, so no mistake occurs at round $t$.
Let $t_1<t_2<\cdots$ be the mistake rounds.
For each $k$, $x_{t_k}\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{x_1,\dots,x_{t_k-1}\})\supseteq\operatorname{cl}(\{x_{t_1},\dots,x_{t_{k-1}}\})$, by monotonicity of $\operatorname{cl}$.
So the points of the mistake rounds, in order, form an irredundant sequence, and there are at most $\mathsf{I}$ of them.
For the lower bound, let $\mathsf{I}<\infty$ and take the shattered mistake tree of depth $\mathsf{I}$ constructed in the proof of \cref{thm:dictionary}(c).
Against a deterministic learner, walk down the tree: at each node, present its point and reveal the label of an out-edge that differs from the learner's prediction (one of the two distinct labels does).
The resulting sequence is a root-to-leaf path, hence realizable, and every round is a mistake.

Since $d\le\mathsf{H}_X(G)$, there are distinct points $a_1,\dots,a_d\in X$ forming an independent set (a subset of an independent set is independent, by monotonicity of $\operatorname{cl}$).
By the proof of \cref{thm:dictionary}(a), $B=\mathcal{H}|_A=\{(ga_1,\dots,ga_d):g\in G\}$ is a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube, and it is finite by~\eqref{eq:F}.
For each $b\in B$ fix $g_b\in G$ with $g_ba_i=b_i$ for all $i$, and let $h_b=g_b|_X$.
Let $D(a_1)=1-(d-1)/m$ and $D(a_i)=1/m$ for $2\le i\le d$; this is a distribution because $m\ge d-1$.
Draw $b$ uniformly from $B$, independently of the sample points and of the learner's randomness, and use the target $h_b$.

Fix $i\in\{2,\dots,d\}$ and let $U_i$ be the event that $a_i$ is not among $x_1,\dots,x_m$.
Condition on the sample points, with $U_i$ holding, and let $J\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\}$ be the set of indices of the points that were drawn.
Given the observed labels $(b_j)_{j\in J}$, the target $b$ is uniform on $B_J=\{b'\in B:b'_j=b_j\text{ for }j\in J\}$.
Partition $B_J$ into classes of words that agree outside coordinate $i$.
Each class lies in $B_J$, because $i\notin J$, and is an $i$-panel of $B$.
So it has at least two words, and their $i$-th coordinates are pairwise distinct.
Hence for every label $y$ at most half of $B_J$ has $b'_i=y$.
The prediction at $a_i$ depends only on the observed sample and the learner's randomness, so it errs with conditional probability at least $1/2$.

Since $\operatorname{er}_D(f)\ge\sum_{i=2}^d\frac1m\mathbf 1[f(a_i)\neq b_i]$, averaging over $b$ gives
\[
\mathbb{E}_b\mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{er}_D(\mathcal A(S_m))\big]\ge\sum_{i=2}^d\frac1m\cdot\mathbb{P}(U_i)\cdot\frac12\ge\frac{d-1}{8m},
\]
because $\mathbb{P}(U_i)=(1-1/m)^m\ge1/4$ for $m\ge2$.
Some $b$ attains at least the average; take $h^\star=h_b$.
For the comparison, take $d=\mathsf{H}$.
\Cref{thm:erm}(a) gives $\mathsf{H}/(m+1)$ for every consistent learner, and $\frac{\mathsf{H}/(m+1)}{(\mathsf{H}-1)/(8m)}<\frac{8\mathsf{H}}{\mathsf{H}-1}\le16$.
If $\mathsf{H}=\infty$, take $d=m+1$.

(d) Put mass $1/m$ on $e_2,\dots,e_d$ and the rest on $e_1$, and draw a uniformly random sign vector $s$ for the target $\mathrm{diag}(s)$.
At an unsampled $e_i$ the sign $s_i$ is independent of the observed labels, so every prediction errs with probability at least $1/2$; each $e_i$ ($i\ge2$) is unsampled with probability $(1-1/m)^m\ge1/4$.

The sets $T=A$ and $T=A\setminus\{a\}$ give $g_1,g_2\in G$ with $g_1=f=g_2$ on $A\setminus\{a\}$, $g_1a=f(a)$ and $g_2a\neq f(a)$; then $g_1^{-1}g_2\inG_{(A\setminus\{a\})}$ moves $a$, so $a\notin\operatorname{cl}(A\setminus\{a\})$, $A$ is independent and $d_G\le\mathsf{H}$.

For each $j$, the factors after $k_{b_j}$ fix $b_j$, so $Pb_j=Q(z)$ with $Q=k_{b_1}\cdots k_{b_{j-1}}$ and $z=k_{b_j}b_j\neq b_j$; as $Q$ fixes $b_j$, $Q(z)\neq b_j$.

body_md:
Every orbit satisfies $|\Gamma\alpha|\le|\Gamma|<\infty$, so~\eqref{eq:F} holds.

(i) An automorphism $\sigma\in\Gamma$ fixes $A$ pointwise if and only if it fixes the field $K(A)$ pointwise.
So $\Gamma_{(A)}=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(A))$, and $\operatorname{cl}(A)=\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(A)))=K(A)$ by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory \citep[Chapter~VI, Theorems~1.1 and~1.2]{lang2002algebra}.

(ii) \Cref{fact:realization} with $U=1$ gives $\theta\in L$ with $\Gamma_\theta=1$.
Then $\operatorname{cl}(\{\theta\})=L$, so $\{\theta\}$ is a relative base.
The empty set is not a relative base, because $\operatorname{cl}(\emptyset)=K\neq L$ when $\Gamma\neq1$.
So $\mathsf{b}_L(\Gamma)=1$, and $\operatorname{TD}(\mathcal{H})=1$ by \cref{thm:dictionary}(d).

(iii) Let $\Delta\le\Gamma$ act on $L$; then $\Delta_{(B)}=\Delta\cap\Gamma_{(B)}$ for $B\subseteq L$.
A finite $A\subseteq L$ is $\Delta$-independent if and only if $\Delta_{(A\setminus\{a\})}=\bigcap_{b\in A\setminus\{a\}}\Delta_b$ is not contained in $\Delta_a$ for every $a\in A$.
We show that the largest size of such a set is $\mu(\Delta)$.
($\le$) Let $A$ be $\Delta$-independent, and pick $g_a\in\big(\bigcap_{b\neq a}\Delta_b\big)\setminus\Delta_a$ for each $a\in A$.
For $b\neq a$ we have $g_b\in\Delta_a$, so $\langle g_b : b\neq a\rangle\le\Delta_a$, which does not contain $g_a$.
The elements $g_a$ are distinct, since $g_a\notin\Delta_a\ni g_b$ for $b\neq a$.
So $\{g_a : a\in A\}$ is an independent subset of $\Delta$ of size $|A|$.
($\ge$) Let $\{g_1,\dots,g_h\}\subseteq\Delta$ be independent, and put $U_i=\langle g_j : j\neq i\rangle\le\Delta$.
By \cref{fact:realization} choose $\alpha_i\in L$ with $\Gamma_{\alpha_i}=U_i$; then $\Delta_{\alpha_i}=\Delta\cap U_i=U_i$.
The subgroups $U_i$ are pairwise distinct, because $g_i\in U_j\setminus U_i$ for $j\neq i$; so the points $\alpha_i$ are distinct.
Moreover $g_i\in\bigcap_{j\neq i}\Delta_{\alpha_j}$ and $g_i\notin U_i=\Delta_{\alpha_i}$, so $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_h\}$ is $\Delta$-independent.
Hence $\mathsf{H}_L(\Delta)=\mu(\Delta)$.
With $\Delta=\Gamma$ and \cref{thm:dictionary}(a), $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})=\mu(\Gamma)$.

(iv) A sequence $(a_1,\dots,a_k)$ is irredundant if and only if the chain $\Gamma\ge\Gamma_{(\{a_1\})}\ge\Gamma_{(\{a_1,a_2\})}\ge\dots\ge\Gamma_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_k\})}$ is strictly decreasing.
Indeed, $a_i\notin\operatorname{cl}(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})$ if and only if $\Gamma_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})}$ moves $a_i$, that is, $\Gamma_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_i\})}\neq\Gamma_{(\{a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\})}$.
A strictly decreasing chain of subgroups that starts at $\Gamma$ can be extended down to $1$, so its length is at most $\ell(\Gamma)$.
Conversely, for a chain $\Gamma=U_0>U_1>\dots>U_\ell=1$, choose $\alpha_i$ with $\Gamma_{\alpha_i}=U_i$ by \cref{fact:realization}.
Then $\Gamma_{(\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_i\})}=\bigcap_{j\le i}U_j=U_i$, so $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_\ell)$ is irredundant.
Hence $\mathsf{I}_L(\Gamma)=\ell(\Gamma)$, and $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})=\ell(\Gamma)$ by \cref{thm:dictionary}(c).

(v) By \cref{lem:coset}(ii), the consistent labels of $\alpha$ are $\sigma(\Gamma_{(A)}\,\alpha)$ for the target $\sigma$, a set of size $|\Gamma_{(A)}\,\alpha|$.
By (i), $\Gamma_{(A)}=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(A))$, and $L/K(A)$ is Galois.
So the orbit of $\alpha$ under $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(A))$ is the set of roots of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K(A)$, which is separable of degree $[K(A)(\alpha):K(A)]$ (\cref{fact:conjugates}).

(vi) By \cref{thm:natarajan}(iii) and by (iii) applied to $\Delta$, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})\ge\mathsf{H}_L(\Delta)=\mu(\Delta)$ for every abelian $\Delta\le\Gamma$.
It remains to compute $\mu$ for a finite abelian group $\Delta$, which we write additively.
($\ge$) Write $\Delta=\bigoplus_{i=1}^rZ_i$ with $Z_i=\langle z_i\rangle$ cyclic of prime-power order, where $r=\sum_pd(\Delta_p)$.
Then $z_i\notin\bigoplus_{j\neq i}Z_j=\langle z_j : j\neq i\rangle$, so $\{z_1,\dots,z_r\}$ is independent.
($\le$) Let $\{h_1,\dots,h_s\}$ be independent, let $N=\langle h_1,\dots,h_s\rangle$ and $B_i=\langle h_j : j\neq i\rangle$.
The quotient $N/B_i$ is cyclic, generated by the image $\bar h_i$ of $h_i$, and nontrivial; choose a prime $p_i$ dividing $|N/B_i|$.
Fix a prime $p$ and let $I_p=\{i : p_i=p\}$.
Suppose that $\sum_{i\in I_p}c_ih_i\in pN$ for integers $0\le c_i<p$, not all zero, say $c_k\neq0$.
Reducing modulo $B_k$ gives $c_k\bar h_k=p\bar n$ for some $\bar n\in N/B_k=\langle\bar h_k\rangle$; writing $\bar n=t\bar h_k$, we get $(c_k-pt)\bar h_k=0$, so the order of $\bar h_k$ divides $c_k-pt$.
Since $p$ divides this order, $p$ divides $c_k$, a contradiction.
So the images of the $h_i$, $i\in I_p$, in $N/pN$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_p$, and $|I_p|\le\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}N/pN=d(N_p)\le d(\Delta_p)$; the last inequality holds because a subgroup of a finite abelian $p$-group needs no more generators than the group.
Summing over $p$ gives $s\le\sum_pd(\Delta_p)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{The matroid.}
The operator $\operatorname{cl}$ is extensive, monotone and idempotent (\cref{lem:closure}).
Together with exchange on the finite set $\Omega$, these are the closure axioms of a matroid on $\Omega$ whose closure operator is $\operatorname{cl}$, and whose independent sets are the sets $I$ with $x\notin\operatorname{cl}(I\setminus\{x\})$ for all $x\in I$ \citep[Section~1.4]{oxley2011matroid}; these are exactly the independent sets of \cref{sec:prelim}.
Let $r$ be its rank function.
We use the standard facts \citep[Sections~1.3--1.4]{oxley2011matroid}: (M0) $r(\operatorname{cl} S)=r(S)$; (M1) $r(S)\le r(S\cup T)\le r(S)+|T|$; (M2) $s\in\operatorname{cl}(T)$ if and only if $r(T\cup\{s\})=r(T)$.
Say that $S$ is \emph{independent over} $F$ if $s\notin\operatorname{cl}(F\cup(S\setminus\{s\}))$ for every $s\in S$.
(M3) If $S$ is independent over $F$, then $r(F\cup S)=r(F)+|S|$: order $S$ as $s_1,\dots,s_k$; by monotonicity $s_i\notin\operatorname{cl}(F\cup\{s_1,\dots,s_{i-1}\})$, so by (M2) each step raises the rank by one.
(M4) For all $F,T$ there is $S\subseteq T$ independent over $F$ with $|S|=r(F\cup T)-r(F)$: scan $T$ and keep an element exactly when it is not in the closure of $F$ together with the elements kept before it.
Every discarded element lies in $\operatorname{cl}(F\cup S)$, so $\operatorname{cl}(F\cup S)=\operatorname{cl}(F\cup T)$ and, by (M0), $r(F\cup S)=r(F\cup T)$.
Each kept element raises the rank by one, so $r(F\cup S)=r(F)+|S|$.
For $s\in S$, (M1) gives $r(F\cup(S\setminus\{s\}))\le r(F)+|S|-1<r(F\cup S)$, so $s\notin\operatorname{cl}(F\cup(S\setminus\{s\}))$ by (M2).

\emph{The recursion.}
Let $A$ be independent with $|A|=h=\mathsf{H}(G)$, and put $F_0=\emptyset$ and $R_1=A$, which is independent over $\emptyset$.
For $j=1,2,\dots$, while $R_j\neq\emptyset$: pick $x_j\in R_j$.
Since $R_j$ is independent over $F_{j-1}$, we have $x_j\notin\operatorname{cl}(F_{j-1}\cup(R_j\setminus\{x_j\}))$, so some $k_j\inG_{(F_{j-1}\cup(R_j\setminus\{x_j\}))}$ moves $x_j$.
Put $x_j'=k_jx_j$ and $F_j=F_{j-1}\cup\{x_j,x_j'\}$.
Since $F_j\cup(R_j\setminus\{x_j\})\supseteq F_{j-1}\cup R_j$, (M1) and (M3) give
\[
r\big(F_j\cup(R_j\setminus\{x_j\})\big)\ \ge\ r(F_{j-1}\cup R_j)\ =\ r(F_{j-1})+|R_j|\ \ge\ r(F_j)-2+|R_j|,
\]
where the last step uses $r(F_j)\le r(F_{j-1})+2$.
By (M4), choose $R_{j+1}\subseteq R_j\setminus\{x_j\}$ independent over $F_j$ with $|R_{j+1}|\ge|R_j|-2$.

\emph{The tower.}
The point $x_j$ is not in $\operatorname{cl}(F_{j-1}\cup(R_j\setminus\{x_j\}))$, a set that contains every earlier point $x_i$ and every later point $x_i$ (the later points lie in $R_{j+1}\subseteq R_j\setminus\{x_j\}$); so the points are distinct.
(T1) holds by the choice of $k_j$.
For $i<j$, both $x_i$ and $x_i'$ lie in $F_{j-1}$, which $k_j$ fixes pointwise: this gives (T2) for $i<j$ and (T3).
For $i>j$, $x_i\in R_i\subseteq R_{j+1}\subseteq R_j\setminus\{x_j\}$, which $k_j$ fixes pointwise: this gives (T2) for $i>j$.
Since $|R_j|\ge h-2(j-1)\ge1$ for all $j\le\lceil h/2\rceil$, the recursion produces at least $\lceil h/2\rceil$ points, and \cref{lem:tower} gives $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H}_{G,\Omega})\ge\lceil h/2\rceil$.

\emph{Tightness.}
For $S_n$ acting on $[n]$, $n\ge2$, the pointwise stabilizer of $A$ is $\operatorname{Sym}([n]\setminus A)$, so $\operatorname{cl}(A)=A$ if $|A|\le n-2$ and $\operatorname{cl}(A)=[n]$ otherwise.
Exchange holds: if $q\in\operatorname{cl}(S\cup\{p\})\setminus\operatorname{cl}(S)$, then $|S|\le n-2$ and $q\notin S$; either $|S\cup\{p\}|\le n-2$, in which case $q\in S\cup\{p\}$ forces $q=p$; or $|S|=n-2<|S\cup\{p\}|$, in which case $|S\cup\{q\}|=n-1$ and $p\in[n]=\operatorname{cl}(S\cup\{q\})$.
For $n=2k+1$, \cref{prop:symmetric}(b) gives $\mathsf{H}=2k$ and $\operatorname{Nat}=k$.

Then $k_ix_i=y_i\neq x_i$, so $k_i\notin V_i$.

Preimages commute with intersections, and the preimage of a nonempty set under a surjection is nonempty.

(iii) Let $(V_i,k_i)_{i\le t}$ be a cube in $Q$ with $t=N(Q)$, and fix $k_0\in M\setminus\{1\}$.
Set $V_0=Q$, and $V_i'=MV_i$ with $k_i'=k_i$ for $i\ge1$; each $MV_i$ is a subgroup because $M$ is normal.
First, $k_0\notin Q$ because $M\cap Q=1$.
Second, by Dedekind's rule, $Q\cap MV_i=(Q\cap M)V_i=V_i$: if $mv\in Q$ with $v\in V_i\subseteq Q$, then $m=(mv)v^{-1}\in Q\cap M$.
Hence $k_i\in Q\setminus V_i$ gives $k_i\notin MV_i$.
Third, given a pattern $(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon)$, pick $g\in\bigcap_{i\ge1}k_i^{\varepsilon_i}V_i\subseteq Q$ (for $t=0$ take $g=1$) and put $w=k_0^{\varepsilon_0}g$.
Then $w\in k_0^{\varepsilon_0}Q$.
For $i\ge1$, the set $k_i^{\varepsilon_i}MV_i=Mk_i^{\varepsilon_i}V_i$ contains $g$ and is closed under left multiplication by elements of $M$, so it contains $w$.

(iv) By (ii) it suffices to show, for every finite group $\Delta$ and every chief series $1=\Delta_0<\Delta_1<\dots<\Delta_r=\Delta$ of $\Delta$, that $N(\Delta)\ge c$, where $c$ is the number of complemented factors of the series; we induct on $|\Delta|$.
For $|\Delta|=1$ both sides are $0$.
Otherwise let $M=\Delta_1$, a minimal normal subgroup, and $\bar\Delta=\Delta/M$.
By the correspondence theorem, $(\Delta_{j+1}/M)_{0\le j<r}$ is a chief series of $\bar\Delta$ whose factors correspond to $\Delta_{j+1}/\Delta_j$.
For $i\ge2$, the factor $\Delta_i/\Delta_{i-1}$ is complemented in $\Delta$ if and only if its image is complemented in $\bar\Delta$.
Indeed, the subgroups $C\supseteq\Delta_{i-1}\supseteq M$ correspond to $C/M$, with $(C/M)(\Delta_i/M)=C\Delta_i/M$ and $(C/M)\cap(\Delta_i/M)=(C\cap\Delta_i)/M$.
So the induced series of $\bar\Delta$ has $\bar c=c-[\Delta_1\text{ complemented}]$ complemented factors, where $[\phi]=1$ if the statement $\phi$ holds and $[\phi]=0$ otherwise, and $N(\bar\Delta)\ge\bar c$ by induction.
If $M$ has a complement $C$, then $C\cong\Delta/M$, and (iii) gives $N(\Delta)\ge N(C)+1=N(\bar\Delta)+1\ge c$.
Otherwise (ii) gives $N(\Delta)\ge N(\bar\Delta)\ge\bar c=c$.
Combined with (i) and (ii), this proves the last statement.

So $S$ is a minimal generating set of $\Delta$.
The group $\Delta$ is solvable, so all its chief factors are abelian, and the following lemma (the inequality half of \citealp[Theorem~2]{lucchini2013largest}) gives $\mu(\Gamma)=|S|\le c$ for the number $c$ of complemented factors of any chief series of $\Delta$.
Then \cref{thm:cosetcube}(iv) gives $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})\ge c\ge\mu(\Gamma)$.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:mingen}
Let $G$ be a finite group with a chief series $1=G_0<G_1<\dots<G_r=G$ whose factors are all abelian, and let $c$ be its number of complemented factors.
Then every minimal generating set $T$ of $G$ has $|T|\le c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induct on $|G|$; for $|G|=1$, $T=\emptyset$.
Let $N=G_1$, an abelian minimal normal subgroup, and $\bar G=G/N$ with the chief series $(G_{j+1}/N)_j$.
For $i\ge2$, the factor $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is complemented in $G$ if and only if its image is complemented in $\bar G$, through $C\leftrightarrow C/N$.
So the series of $\bar G$ has $\bar c=c-[N\text{ complemented}]$ complemented factors.
Choose $T'\subseteq T$ minimal with $\langle T'\rangle N=G$.
The images of $T'$ are distinct and form a minimal generating set of $\bar G$, so $|T'|\le\bar c$ by induction.
For $z\in T\setminus T'$, put $M_z=\langle T\setminus\{z\}\rangle$.
Then $M_zN=G$ and $M_z\ne G$.
The intersection $M_z\cap N$ is normalized by $M_z$ and centralized by the abelian $N$, so it is normal in $G$; it is not $N$, hence $M_z\cap N=1$, and $M_z$ complements $N$.
Suppose $x\ne y$ both lie in $T\setminus T'$, and let $K=\langle T\setminus\{x,y\}\rangle$.
Then $KN=G$ and $K\cap N\le M_x\cap N=1$, so $|K|=|M_x|$.
Hence $K=M_x\ni y$, so $T\setminus\{y\}$ generates $G$, contradicting minimality.
So $|T\setminus T'|\le1$, with equality only if $N$ is complemented, and $|T|\le\bar c+[N\text{ complemented}]=c$.
\end{proof}

(c) The upper bound is \cref{cor:galois-values}(a) together with $\operatorname{Nat}\le\operatorname{DS}$ (for $n=1$ both dimensions are~$0$).
For the lower bound, first $N(\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2)\ge N(\Gamma_1)+N(\Gamma_2)$.
Indeed, cubes $(V_i,k_i)$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $(U_j,l_j)$ in $\Gamma_2$ give the cube consisting of $(V_i\times\Gamma_2,(k_i,1))$ and $(\Gamma_1\times U_j,(1,l_j))$, whose intersections are products of nonempty sets.
We have $N(S_2)=1$.
By \cref{thm:cosetcube}(iv), $N(S_3)\ge2$, using the series $1<A_3<S_3$, where $A_3$ is complemented by a transposition.
Likewise $N(S_4)\ge3$, using the series $1<V_4<A_4<S_4$: $V_4$ is complemented by a point stabilizer $S_3$, and $A_4/V_4$ by $D_4$, since $D_4\cap A_4=V_4$ and $|D_4||A_4|/|V_4|=24$.
In both series the top factor is complemented by the previous term.
Write $n=4a+\rho$ with $0\le\rho\le3$.
Disjoint blocks give a subgroup $S_4^a\times S_3^{[\rho=3]}\times S_2^{[\rho=2]}\le S_n$.
So $N(S_n)\ge3a+[\rho=2]+2[\rho=3]=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, and \cref{thm:cosetcube}(i) converts this to $\operatorname{Nat}$.

(b) Here $\mu(A_5)\ge3$: the elements $u_1=(2\,3\,4)$, $u_2=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ and $u_3=(0\,1)(3\,4)$ of $A_5$ on $\{0,\dots,4\}$ are independent.
Indeed, $\langle u_2,u_3\rangle$ preserves the partition $\{0,1,2\}\mid\{3,4\}$ but $u_1$ does not; $\langle u_1,u_3\rangle$ preserves $\{0,1\}\mid\{2,3,4\}$ but $u_2$ does not; and $\langle u_1,u_2\rangle$ fixes $0$ but $u_3$ does not.
For $S_5$, the transpositions $(1\,2),(2\,3),(3\,4),(4\,5)$ are independent, and $\operatorname{DS}=4$ by \cref{cor:galois-values}(a).
Next, $N(A_5)\ge2$.
Take $V_0=\langle(0\,1\,2)\rangle$ with $k_0=(0\,1)(2\,3)$, and $V_1=\{1,(0\,1)(2\,3),(0\,2)(1\,3),(0\,3)(1\,2)\}$ with $k_1=(0\,1\,2)$.
The four patterns contain $1$, $k_0$, $k_1$ and $k_0k_1$ respectively; for the last, $k_1^{-1}k_0k_1\in V_1$ because $V_1$ is normal in the stabilizer $A_4$ of the point $4$.
Also $N(S_5)\ge3$: in $S_5$ acting on $\{0,\dots,4\}$, the subgroups $V_1=\langle(1\,2),(3\,4)\rangle$, $V_2=\langle(0\,1\,2),(3\,4)\rangle$ and $V_3=\mathrm{Sym}\{0,1,2\}$, with $k_1=(0\,1)$, $k_2=(1\,2)$ and $k_3=(3\,4)$, form a coset cube; this is also part~(c).
The upper bounds $N(A_5)\le2$, $\mu(A_5)\le3$ and $N(S_5)\le3$ are \cref{lem:quintic} below.
By (i) of \cref{thm:cosetcube} and \cref{thm:galois}(iii), this gives $\operatorname{Nat}=2<3=\operatorname{DS}$ for $A_5$ and $\operatorname{Nat}=3<4=\operatorname{DS}$ for $S_5$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Groups act on the left.
Restricting a cube to some of its coordinates gives a cube, and subsets of independent sets are independent.
So it suffices to exclude a $3$-cube in $A_5$, an independent $4$-set in $A_5$ and a $4$-cube in $S_5$.
For a $t$-cube $(V_i;k_i)$ pick $g_\varepsilon$ in the cell of $\varepsilon$, with $g_0=1$.
We use three facts.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(Q1)] The $V_i$ are pairwise incomparable: if $V_i\le V_j$, the pattern with $\varepsilon_i=0$ and $\varepsilon_j=1$ needs an element of $V_j\cap k_jV_j=\emptyset$.
\item[(Q2)] \emph{Face lemma.} For fixed $i$, the subgroups $W_j=V_i\cap V_j$ ($j\ne i$) with the elements $g_{e_j}\in V_i$ form a $(t-1)$-cube inside $V_i$.
Indeed, $V_i\cap k_jV_j=g_{e_j}(V_i\cap V_j)$, because it contains $g_{e_j}$.
By (Q1) inside $V_i$, the $W_j$ are pairwise incomparable, hence nontrivial and proper when $t-1\ge2$.
\item[(Q3)] Two distinct subgroups $\langle s\rangle,\langle s'\rangle$ of order $2$ carry a $2$-cube only if $ss'=s's$.
Indeed, the cells force $g_{10}=s'$ and $g_{01}=s$, and $g_{11}\in\{s',s's\}\cap\{s,ss'\}$.
In $A_4$, an involution subgroup $\langle a\rangle$ and a subgroup $\langle c\rangle$ of order~$3$ carry no $2$-cube, since the cells would force $a\in N_{A_4}(\langle c\rangle)=\langle c\rangle$, where $N_H(U)$ denotes the normalizer of a subgroup $U$ in a group $H$.
\end{itemize}

\emph{No $3$-cube in $A_5$.}
Each $V_i$ is proper and, by (Q2), contains two incomparable nontrivial proper subgroups, so it is $V_4$, $S_3$, $D_5$ or $A_4$.
Call the $V_i$ the \emph{vertices} of the cube and the subgroups $W_{ij}=V_i\cap V_j$ its \emph{edges}; the edges at each vertex carry a $2$-cube.
Two edges at a vertex are distinct subgroups, and distinct reflections of $S_3$ and $D_5$ do not commute.
So by (Q3) the edge types at a vertex are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\{C_2,C_2\}$ at $V_4$;
\item $\{C_2,C_3\}$ at $S_3$;
\item $\{C_2,C_5\}$ at $D_5$;
\item $\{C_2,C_2\}$, $\{C_3,C_3\}$ or $\{V_4,C_3\}$ at $A_4$.
\end{itemize}
In $A_5$ there is no $C_5$ edge, since a $C_5$ lies only in $N_{A_5}(C_5)\cong D_5$; so no vertex is $D_5$.
There is no $V_4$ edge, since the subgroups containing a $V_4$ are $V_4$ and $N_{A_5}(V_4)\cong A_4$, which are nested.
No $C_3$ edge joins two $S_3$ vertices, since $N_{A_5}(C_3)$ is the only $S_3$ containing a given $C_3$.
Every $V_4$ is the set $V_4^{(q)}$ of double transpositions fixing a point $q$, together with $1$.
Every $A_4$ is a point stabilizer $\mathrm{Stab}(q)=(A_5)_q$; we also write $\mathrm{Stab}(p,q)=(A_5)_{(\{p,q\})}$ for the pointwise stabilizer of two points.
Since $V_4^{(q)}$ meets every other $V_4$ and every $\mathrm{Stab}(p)$ with $p\ne q$ trivially, a $V_4$ vertex would need two $S_3$ neighbours.
Each of those would then need a $C_3$ edge to the other, which is impossible.
So every vertex is $S_3$ or $\mathrm{Stab}(p)$; let $s$ be the number of $S_3$ vertices.
\begin{itemize}
\item $s=3$ is impossible, since an $S_3$ needs a $C_3$ edge to a vertex that is not an $S_3$.
\item If $s=2$, the $A_4$ vertex $\mathrm{Stab}(p)$ has edges $\mathrm{Stab}(p,q)$ and $\mathrm{Stab}(p,r)$ with $q\ne r$, and the two $S_3$ vertices are their normalizers.
Every involution of $N_{A_5}(\mathrm{Stab}(p,q))$ contains the transposition $(p\,q)$, and every involution of $N_{A_5}(\mathrm{Stab}(p,r))$ contains $(p\,r)$.
So the common edge of the two $S_3$ vertices contains no involution, contradicting its type $C_2$.
\item If $s=1$, two point stabilizers meet in a $C_3$.
This forces both of their edges to the $S_3$ vertex to be $C_3$, again impossible.
\item If $s=0$, then $V_i=\mathrm{Stab}(p_i)$; put $q_i=k_ip_i$.
The pattern $\varepsilon$ requires $g_\varepsilon(p_i)\in\{p_i,q_i\}$ according to $\varepsilon_i$.
Injectivity of $g_\varepsilon$ forces the pairs $\{p_i,q_i\}$ to be pairwise disjoint, which needs $6$ points.
\end{itemize}

\emph{No independent $4$-set in $A_5$.}
An independent $k$-set gives a strict chain of subgroups of length $k$.
A chain in $H$ has length at most $\omega^{+}(|H|)$, the number of prime factors of $|H|$ counted with multiplicity (\cref{sec:fields}).
Suppose $S\subseteq A_5$ is independent with $|S|=4$.
Then each $3$-subset generates a proper subgroup with a chain of length $3$, which must be an $A_4$.
Every such chain in $A_4$ passes through its $V_4$, since $A_4$ has no subgroup of order~$6$.
So every pair from the $3$-subset generates $V_4$, which puts the whole $3$-subset inside $V_4$, a contradiction.

\emph{No $4$-cube in $S_5$.}
By (Q2), each $V_i$ carries a $3$-cube.
So $|V_i|\ge8$, and $V_i$ has three pairwise incomparable proper subgroups, each carrying a $2$-cube.
We list the proper subgroups $H$ of $S_5$ with $|H|\ge8$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $H$ is intransitive with orbits $4+1$, it lies in a point stabilizer and is $D_4$, $A_4$ or $S_4$.
\item If $H$ is intransitive with orbits $3+2$, it is the stabilizer $S_3\times S_2$ of a $2$-set.
\item Finer orbit partitions give $|H|\le6$.
\item If $H$ is transitive, then $5$ divides $|H|$. A normal Sylow $5$-subgroup puts $H$ inside its normalizer, the Frobenius group $F_{20}=\mathrm{AGL}(1,5)$ of order $20$, so $H$ is $D_5$ or $F_{20}$. Otherwise $30$ divides $|H|$, and $H=A_5$, because $A_5$ has no subgroup of order $15$ or $30$.
\end{itemize}
Of these, $D_4$ has only its two Klein subgroups carrying a $2$-cube, $D_5$ has none, $A_4$ has one and $F_{20}$ has one.
Also $N(A_5)\le2$.
So each $V_i$ is the stabilizer of an object $x_i$, which is a point or a $2$-set.
Put $y_i=k_ix_i\ne x_i$.
The pattern $\varepsilon$ requires $g_\varepsilon(x_i)=x_i$ or $y_i$ according to $\varepsilon_i$.
Comparing the patterns $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ on two coordinates gives three rules.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(S1)] Two point objects have disjoint pairs $\{x_i,y_i\}$ and $\{x_j,y_j\}$.
\item[(S2)] A point object lies outside every $2$-set object. Moreover, the point and its image both avoid the $2$-set and its image.
\item[(S3)] Two $2$-set objects meet in exactly one point. If they were disjoint, the fifth point would lie in both images.
\end{itemize}
Let $\nu$ be the number of point objects among the four.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\nu\ge3$ needs $6$ points.
\item $\nu=2$ leaves a single point for any $2$-set object.
\item $\nu=1$ confines two $2$-set objects and their two images, four distinct $2$-sets, to a $3$-set.
\item $\nu=0$ gives four pairwise-intersecting $2$-sets, which form a star $\{v,a_1\},\dots,\{v,a_4\}$.
The element realizing the first unit pattern fixes the other three sets setwise.
So it fixes $v,a_2,a_3,a_4$ and hence $a_1$, so it is the identity, contradicting $y_1\ne x_1$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
The translations $z\mapsto z+b$, $b\in\mathbb F_8$, form a subgroup $E\cong C_2^3$ of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$.
A basis $t_1,t_2,t_3$ of $E$ is an independent set, so $\mu\ge3$.
The chief series $1<\langle t_1\rangle<\langle t_1,t_2\rangle<E$ has three complemented factors, so $N\ge N(E)\ge3$ by \cref{thm:cosetcube}(ii) and~(iv).
Moreover $N\le\mu$ for every finite group: given a coset cube $(V_i,k_i)_{i\le t}$, pick $g_i$ in the cell of the $i$-th unit pattern; then $g_i\notin V_i$ while $g_j\in V_i$ for $j\neq i$, so $\langle g_j:j\neq i\rangle\le V_i\not\ni g_i$, the $g_i$ are distinct, and $\{g_1,\dots,g_t\}$ is independent.
Finally $\mu\le3$; we argue by hand, using Dickson's list of maximal subgroups and sharp $3$-transitivity (an exhaustive computer search, with several independent programs, confirms the value).
(For comparison, \citet{whiston2002psl} bound the size of independent generating sets of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(q)$; our $\mu$ counts all independent subsets.)
Write $T=\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$, acting on the projective line $\mathbb F_8\cup\{\infty\}$.
Since $8$ is even, every element of $\mathbb F_8^\times$ is a square, so $T$, the group of M\"obius maps $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ with $ad-bc$ a nonzero square, is all of $\mathrm{PGL}(2,8)$ \citep[Section~2]{cameron2006designs} \citep[see also][p.~3]{leemans2009pgl}.
It acts $3$-transitively on the $9$ points and has order $504=9\cdot8\cdot7$ \citep[Section~2]{cameron2006designs}, so the action is sharply $3$-transitive, and a nonidentity element fixes at most two points.
Every maximal subgroup of $T$ is isomorphic to $C_2^3\rtimes C_7$, $D_7$ or $D_9$, of orders $56$, $14$ and $18$ \citep[Theorem~2.1]{giudici2007maximal}.
Independence of a set does not depend on the ambient group, and subsets of independent sets are independent.
\emph{Dihedral groups.} In $D_m$ with $m\in\{7,9\}$, two rotations are dependent, since the subgroups of a cyclic group of prime-power order form a chain; two reflections $u,v$ generate $\langle uv,u\rangle$, which is all of $D_m$ unless $m=9$ and $uv$ has order $3$; in that case a third element outside $\langle uv,u\rangle$ generates $D_m$ together with $u$. So no $3$-subset is independent, and $\mu(D_7)=\mu(D_9)=2$.
\emph{Point stabilizers.} $T_\infty=\{z\mapsto az+b\}$, with the normal subgroup $E$ of translations, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $T$ (as $|T|=504=8\cdot63$).
A nonidentity translation fixes only $\infty$, so an element $g$ that normalizes $E$ satisfies $g\infty=\infty$ (the nonidentity elements of $gEg^{-1}$ fix $g\infty$); since $E$ is normal in $T_\infty$, the normalizer of $E$ is $T_\infty$.
A subgroup of $T$ of order $56$ isomorphic to $C_2^3\rtimes C_7$ normalizes its normal subgroup of order $8$, a conjugate $gEg^{-1}$, so it lies in $gT_\infty g^{-1}=T_{g\infty}$ and, having the same order, equals it: it is a point stabilizer.
An element $x\colon z\mapsto az+b$ with $a\neq1$ has order $7$, and conjugation by $x$ multiplies translations by $a$; since $\mathbb F_2[a]=\mathbb F_8$, the only $x$-invariant subgroups of $E$ are $1$ and $E$.
Hence, if a subgroup $K\le T_\infty$ is not contained in $E$, it contains such an $x$, and $K\cap E$, being $x$-invariant, is $1$ or $E$. If $K\cap E=E$, then $K\supseteq\langle E,x\rangle=T_\infty$, since $8$ and $7$ divide $|\langle E,x\rangle|$. If $K\cap E=1$, then $|K|=|KE|/|E|\le7$, so $K=\langle x\rangle$. So every proper subgroup of $T_\infty$ lies in $E$ or is cyclic of order $7$.
If $S\subseteq T_\infty$ were independent with $|S|=4$, then $S\not\subseteq E$ (four vectors in $\mathbb F_2^3$ are dependent); for $s_1\in S\setminus E$ and two other elements $s_2,s_3$, the proper subgroups $\langle S\setminus\{s_2\}\rangle$ and $\langle S\setminus\{s_3\}\rangle$ contain $s_1$, so both equal $\langle s_1\rangle$, and $s_2\in\langle s_1\rangle\subseteq\langle S\setminus\{s_2\}\rangle$, a contradiction. So $\mu(T_\infty)=3$, and hence $\mu(T_p)=3$ for every point $p$, as all point stabilizers are conjugate.
\emph{The group $T$.} Let $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_4\}\subseteq T$ be independent and $M_i=\langle S\setminus\{s_i\}\rangle$.
Each $M_i$ is proper, so it lies in a maximal subgroup of $T$; that subgroup contains the independent $3$-set $S\setminus\{s_i\}$, so by the dihedral paragraph it is not isomorphic to $D_7$ or $D_9$, so it has order $56$ and is a point stabilizer $T_{p_i}$, by the paragraph on point stabilizers.
If the $p_i$ are pairwise distinct, each $s_k$ lies in the three groups $M_i$ with $i\neq k$ and fixes three points, so $s_k=1$, which no independent set contains.
If $p_i=p_j$ for some $i\neq j$, then $S\subseteq M_i\cup M_j\subseteq T_{p_i}$, contradicting $\mu(T_{p_i})=3$.
The statement about $\mathcal{H}_{\Gamma,L}$ follows from \cref{thm:cosetcube}(i) and \cref{thm:galois}(iii).

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonality}
Let $(V_i,k_i)_{i\le t}$ be a $2$-full family in $S_n$, and let $g_i$ be as in \cref{lem:unitcells}.
Let $i\neq j$, and let $A,A'\subseteq[n]$ satisfy $V_iA=A$ and $V_jA'=A'$.
Then $\langle\mathbf 1_{g_iA}-\mathbf 1_A,\ \mathbf 1_{g_jA'}-\mathbf 1_{A'}\rangle=0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}$ pick $h\in C_{\alpha e_i+\beta e_j}$.
Then $h\in k_i^\alpha V_i=g_i^\alpha V_i$, so $hA=g_i^\alpha A$; likewise $hA'=g_j^\beta A'$.
Hence $|g_i^\alpha A\cap g_j^\beta A'|=|h(A\cap A')|=|A\cap A'|$ does not depend on $(\alpha,\beta)$.
Expanding, the inner product is $|g_iA\cap g_jA'|-|g_iA\cap A'|-|A\cap g_jA'|+|A\cap A'|=0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the transpositions along the edges of a graph on $[n]$ generate a group containing every transposition inside a connected component, since $(x\,y)(y\,z)(x\,y)=(x\,z)$.
Suppose $v\in V$ and $a\in A$ have $b=v(a)\in B$.
Since $|A|+|v(A)|>n$, some $x$ lies in $A\cap v(A)$; then $x\neq b$ and $(x\,b)\in\operatorname{Sym}(v(A))=v\,\operatorname{Sym}(A)\,v^{-1}\le V$.
So $V$ contains all transpositions inside $A$, all inside $B$, and $(x\,b)$, which connect $[n]$; hence $V=S_n$.
