title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n\ge5$ and suppose that $(V_i,k_i)_{i\le n-1}$ is a $2$-full family in $S_n$.
By \cref{lem:unitcells}, $S=\{g_1,\dots,g_{n-1}\}$ is an independent subset of $S_n$ of size $n-1$.
By the theorem of \citet{whiston2000maximal}, an independent subset of $S_n$ of size $n-1$ generates $S_n$ (see also \citealp[Section~2]{cameron2002independent}); so $S$ generates $S_n$.
By \citet[Theorem~2.1]{cameron2002independent}, for $n\ge7$, there are a tree $T$ on $[n]$ and an edge $s=(a\,b)$ of~$T$ such that, writing $S(T)$ for the transpositions along the edges of~$T$, either $S=S(T)$ or $S=\{s\}\cup\{(st)^{\pm1}:t\in S(T)\setminus\{s\}\}$.
By the remark following their Corollary~2.4, the same holds for $n=5$, and for $n=6$ it holds after applying an automorphism of $S_6$; an automorphism maps cosets to cosets and preserves intersections and non-membership, so we may apply it to the whole family.
If $t$ is disjoint from $s$ then $st=ts$, and otherwise $(st)^{-1}=ts$.
So in all cases $S=\{s\}\cup\{g_t:t\in S(T)\setminus\{s\}\}$ with $g_t\in\{t,st,ts\}$ (for $S=S(T)$, take any edge as $s$ and $g_t=t$).
The $n-1$ elements of $S$ are distinct (\cref{lem:unitcells}) and $T$ has $n-1$ edges, so $s$ and the $g_t$ ($t\neq s$) are distinct and exhaust~$S$.
We index the family by the edges of~$T$, so that $g_s=s$ and $g_t$ is the element chosen from the unit cell of the coordinate indexed by~$t$.

For an edge $t\neq s$, the endpoints $a,b$ of $s$ lie in one component $B_t$ of $T-t$; let $A_t$ be the other component, $x_t\in A_t$ the endpoint of $t$ in $A_t$, and $y_t\in B_t$ its other endpoint.
Every generator in $S\setminus\{g_t\}$ preserves $A_t$ and $B_t$, and the group they generate contains $s$, hence every $t'\in S(T)\setminus\{t\}$; so $\langle S\setminus\{g_t\}\rangle=\operatorname{Sym}(A_t)\times\operatorname{Sym}(B_t)$.
By \cref{lem:unitcells} this group lies in $V_t$, and $V_t\neq S_n$.
Call $t$ \emph{balanced} if $|A_t|=|B_t|$.
If $t$ is unbalanced, \cref{lem:young}, applied to the larger of $A_t,B_t$, gives $V_tA_t=A_t$.
Since $s$ fixes $A_t$ pointwise and $t$ fixes $A_t\setminus\{x_t\}$ pointwise, $g_tA_t=(A_t\setminus\{x_t\})\cup\{y'_t\}$ with $y'_t=g_t(x_t)\in B_t$.
If $y_t\notin\{a,b\}$ then $y'_t=y_t$, and if $y_t\in\{a,b\}$ (we say that $t$ \emph{touches}~$s$) then $y'_t\in\{a,b\}$.
Put $d_t=\mathbf 1_{y'_t}-\mathbf 1_{x_t}$.
By \cref{lem:orthogonality}, $\langle d_t,d_{t'}\rangle=0$ for distinct unbalanced edges $t,t'\neq s$.
This has three consequences (\cref{fig:orthogonality}).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(R1)] Let $t,t'$ be distinct unbalanced edges touching~$s$. Their endpoints $x_t,x_{t'}$ are distinct (otherwise $T$ would contain a cycle through~$s$) and lie outside $\{a,b\}$, so $\langle d_t,d_{t'}\rangle=[y'_t=y'_{t'}]$ and hence $y'_t\neq y'_{t'}$. As $y'_t\in\{a,b\}$, at most two unbalanced edges touch~$s$.
\item[(R2)] If $t'$ does not touch $s$, let $t$ be the first edge on the path from $y_{t'}$ to~$a$; then $t\neq s$, $x_t=y_{t'}$ and $A_{t'}\subseteq A_t$. Now $d_{t'}=\mathbf 1_{x_t}-\mathbf 1_{x_{t'}}$, and $y'_t\in B_t$ differs from $x_t$ and from $x_{t'}\in A_t$, while $x_t=y_{t'}\neq x_{t'}$, so $\langle d_t,d_{t'}\rangle=-1$. Hence $t$ and $t'$ are not both unbalanced.
\item[(R3)] Two distinct edges $t,t'\neq s$ that do not touch $s$ and have $y_t=y_{t'}=w$ have $\langle d_t,d_{t'}\rangle=\langle\mathbf 1_w-\mathbf 1_{x_t},\mathbf 1_w-\mathbf 1_{x_{t'}}\rangle=1$, so they are not both unbalanced.
\end{itemize}
A tree has at most one balanced edge: for two balanced edges $e,f$, the side of $e$ away from $f$ and the side of $f$ away from $e$ are disjoint, have $n/2$ points each, and miss an endpoint of~$e$.
Suppose an edge $\beta\neq s$ is balanced.
Then every other edge is unbalanced, so by (R2) every edge inside $A_\beta$ has $x_\beta$ as its endpoint nearer to~$s$ (such an edge does not touch $s$, and the first edge on its path to $a$ is $\beta$ or another, unbalanced, edge inside $A_\beta$), and by (R3) there is at most one such edge.
As $A_\beta$ spans a subtree, $|A_\beta|\le2$, so $n=2|A_\beta|\le4$, a contradiction.
So every edge other than $s$ is unbalanced, by (R2) every such edge touches~$s$, and by (R1) there are at most two of them.
But $T$ has $n-2\ge3$ edges other than~$s$.
This contradiction proves the first statement of~(a).
If $N(S_n)\ge n-1$, the first $n-1$ members of a cube of dimension at least $n-1$ would form a family whose cells contain cells of the cube; so $N(S_n)\le n-2$.

For (b), $S_n$ is the Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ over its fixed field, a countable field, by Artin's theorem \citep[Corollary~3.11]{milne2022fields}, so \cref{thm:cosetcube}(i) and \cref{thm:solvable}(c) give $N(S_n)\ge\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, which equals $n-2$ for $5\le n\le8$.
For (c), $\operatorname{DS}(\mathcal{H})=n-1$ by \cref{thm:solvable}(c); if $n\le4$, then $S_n$ is solvable and \cref{thm:solvable}(a) applies; if $n\ge5$, then $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal{H})=N(S_n)\le n-2$ by \cref{thm:cosetcube}(i) and~(a).
For $X_0$, use \cref{thm:solvable}(d).

body_md:
(a) The word $s_i(b)$ is an $i$-neighbor of $b$, and $b$ is an $i$-neighbor of $s_i(b)$, since the two words differ exactly in coordinate $i$.
By uniqueness of $i$-neighbors, $s_i(s_ib)=b$; and $s_ib\neq b$.
For $i\neq j$, the word $s_ib$ agrees with $b$ in coordinate $j$, so $\pi_j\circ s_i=\pi_j$.
Hence $\pi_j$ is invariant under the group $K_j$ generated by the $s_i$ with $i\neq j$, that is, $\pi_j$ is constant on $K_j$-orbits.
Further, $\pi_j(s_jb)\neq\pi_j(b)$ by the definition of a $j$-neighbor.
If $s_jb\in K_j\cdot b$, then $\pi_j(s_jb)=\pi_j(b)$, a contradiction; so $s_jb\notin K_j\cdot b$, and in particular $s_j\notin K_j$.

(b) If $\iota(b)=\iota(b')$, then $b'\in K_j\cdot b$ for every $j$, so $\pi_j(b')=\pi_j(b)$ for every $j$ by (a), and $b=b'$ because $B\subseteq Y^d$.
The set $B^\sharp=\iota(B)$ is finite and nonempty.
For $j\neq i$ we have $K_j\cdot(s_ib)=K_j\cdot b$, since $s_i\in K_j$; and $K_i\cdot(s_ib)\neq K_i\cdot b$ by separation.
So $\iota(s_ib)$ is an $i$-neighbor of $\iota(b)$, and $B^\sharp$ is a pseudo-cube.
The maps $K_j\cdot b\mapsto\pi_j(b)$ are well defined by (a), and together they send $\iota(b)$ to $b$.

(c) For $m\in M$ write $w(m)=(K_1m,\dots,K_dm)$.
The word $w(s_im)$ agrees with $w(m)$ at every $j\neq i$, because $s_i\in K_j$ gives $K_js_im=K_jm$.
It differs from $w(m)$ at $i$, because $s_im\in K_im$ would mean $s_i\in K_i$, which is false by (a).
The set $C$ is finite, since $M\le\operatorname{Sym}(B)$ is finite, and nonempty; so $C$ is a $d$-dimensional pseudo-cube.
Under $m\mapsto m^{-1}$, right cosets $K_jm$ become left cosets $m^{-1}K_j$, which gives the coset complex $\mathcal{C}_M(K_1,\dots,K_d)$; and $s_i\in\big(\bigcap_{j\neq i}K_j\big)\setminus K_i$ is condition~(1) of \citet[Theorem~45]{brukhim2022characterization}.

The map $K_jm\mapsto K_j\cdot(mb_0)$ is well defined: if $K_jm=K_jm'$, then $m'=km$ with $k\in K_j$, so $m'b_0=k(mb_0)\in K_j\cdot(mb_0)$ and the two orbits coincide.
Applied coordinatewise, these maps send $w(m)$ to $(K_1\cdot(mb_0),\dots,K_d\cdot(mb_0))=\iota(mb_0)$.
Since $M$ is transitive, every $\iota(b)$ is hit, so $C$ is mapped onto $B^\sharp$.

Now let $M$ act regularly, so that $m\mapsto mb_0$ is a bijection from $M$ onto $B$.
Each coordinate map is injective: if $K_j\cdot(mb_0)=K_j\cdot(m'b_0)$, then $m'b_0=kmb_0$ for some $k\in K_j$, so $m'=km$ by regularity, and $K_jm'=K_jm$.
The map on words is injective as well: if $\iota(mb_0)=\iota(m'b_0)$, then $mb_0=m'b_0$ because $\iota$ is injective, so $m=m'$.
Hence the coordinatewise maps are bijections and $C\cong B^\sharp$.

(d) ($\Rightarrow$) Let $M$ be abelian and $b\in B$.
Since $M$ is generated by the commuting involutions $s_i$, we have $M=\{s^\epsilon : \epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d\}$, where $s^\epsilon=\prod_is_i^{\epsilon_i}$.
The map $\epsilon\mapsto s^\epsilon b$ is injective.
Indeed, suppose $s^\epsilon b=s^{\epsilon'}b$ with $\epsilon\neq\epsilon'$, let $\eta=\epsilon+\epsilon'$ modulo $2$, and pick $i$ with $\eta_i=1$.
Then $s^\eta=s^{\epsilon'}s^\epsilon$, so $s^\eta b=b$.
Write $s^\eta=s_ir$ with $r\in K_i$; then $rb=s_ib$, which contradicts separation.
Hence $|Mb|=2^d$.
For $j\in[d]$ write $s^\epsilon=r's_j^{\epsilon_j}$ with $r'\in K_j$; then $\pi_j(s^\epsilon b)=\pi_j(s_j^{\epsilon_j}b)\in\{\pi_j(b),\pi_j(s_jb)\}$, and these two values are distinct by (a).
So the injective map $b'\mapsto(\pi_1(b'),\dots,\pi_d(b'))$ sends $Mb$ into $\prod_j\{\pi_j(b),\pi_j(s_jb)\}$, a set of size $2^d=|Mb|$, and $Mb$ is this product.
Since $B$ is the disjoint union of its $M$-orbits, $B$ is a disjoint union of full Natarajan cubes, and these are the $M$-orbits.
The group $M$ is generated by commuting involutions, so it is an elementary abelian $2$-group.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $B=\bigsqcup_rQ_r$ with $Q_r=\prod_j\{u^r_j,v^r_j\}$ and $u^r_j\neq v^r_j$.
For $b\in Q_r$, the element of $Q_r$ obtained by flipping coordinate $i$ is an $i$-neighbor of $b$ in $B$; since $B$ is two-fibered, it equals $s_ib$.
So each $s_i$ preserves every $Q_r$ and acts on it by flipping coordinate $i$.
These actions commute, so $M$ is abelian, and every element of $M$ has order at most $2$.
The sets $Q_r$ are the $M$-orbits, since $M$ acts transitively on each of them by flips.

(e) Let $M_T=\langle s_i : i\in T\rangle$; it preserves the orbit $O=M_T\cdot b$.
Since the $s_i$ with $i\in T$ commute as maps on $O$, every element of $M_T$ agrees on $O$ with some $s^\epsilon=\prod_{i\in T}s_i^{\epsilon_i}$, $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^T$.
If $s^\epsilon b=s^{\epsilon'}b$ with $\epsilon\neq\epsilon'$, the argument of (d), evaluated on $O$ and using $K_i\supseteq\langle s_j : j\in T\setminus\{i\}\rangle$, contradicts separation; so $|O|=2^{|T|}$.
For $j\in T$, write $s^\epsilon=r's_j^{\epsilon_j}$ on $O$, where $r'$ is a product of the $s_i$ with $i\in T\setminus\{j\}$; each such $s_i$ preserves $\pi_j$, so $\pi_j(s^\epsilon b)=\pi_j(s_j^{\epsilon_j}b)$.
Hence the projection of $s^\epsilon b$ to the coordinates in $T$ is the element of $\prod_{j\in T}\{\pi_j(b),\pi_j(s_jb)\}$ indexed by $\epsilon$, and the projection of $O$ is this whole product, whose factors have two distinct entries by (a).
So the coordinates in $T$ are N-shattered by $B$, with $f_0(j)=\pi_j(b)$ and $f_1(j)=\pi_j(s_jb)$, and $\operatorname{Nat}(B)\ge|T|$.
